A · A room with the window open

A / 01 A room with the window open In the accounts collected by ethnographers in Russian villages from the middle of the nineteenth century onward, death is registered less as an event than as a series of adjustments to a house. Covering mirrors and reflective surfaces (or turning them to the wall) is documented across Russian and East Slavic regions (Tolstaya 1999, pp. 321–324). Informants give two consistent reasons: preventing the 'doubling' of death (if the dead or living are reflected, death will claim another member of the household) and guarding a permeable portal between worlds, lest the wandering soul become trapped or an unquiet spirit enter. Looking into a mirror in a house where a corpse lies was strictly tabooed. Access to the room in the first hours was also regulated: pregnant women and small children were kept away so that the border would not harm unborn or fragile life, and close blood kin did not touch or wash the body (Kremleva 1999, pp. 517–519). Water that stood in the house at the moment of death was poured out and not drunk, because the dead person might have drunk it (Zelenin 1991, p. 349). The body is washed and laid on a bench, feet toward the door, men to the right of the entrance and women to the left; the table is a recent habit, chiefly Belarusian, and some Russian Old Believers lay the dead with the feet toward the icons (Zelenin 1991, pp. 347–348). At the moment of death the stove flues or a small window are opened and a piece of linen or a towel is hung out of the window; Zelenin reports three popular readings: the soul wipes itself with it, wipes its tears, or rests on it (p. 346). A stopped clock is often named, but no source read for this edition records it, so it is not asserted. These are the practices most often repeated in the literature, and they are the ones most often flattened into a single ‘Russian custom’. The sources do not support that flattening. They record variants; they record disagreement between villages a day’s walk apart; and they record the informant’s own uncertainty about why a thing was done. Barsov’s first volume (1872), from the Olonets North, describes the same room with differences. The dead person is laid on straw spread on the bench in the front corner, head toward the icons, with copper coins on the eyes; the house is kept quiet and is either not swept or swept toward the dead, so that others do not die (p. 303). Zelenin’s account above has the feet toward the door, so the two sources disagree on orientation and neither makes a rule. Barsov also says that a piece of linen was hung outside the window, or toward the outer front corner, for forty days after a death, and calls the custom general in Novgorod province; in Korela, when the priest was seen approaching, the window frame was taken out and a patterned towel hung there, because the dead were believed to enter a house through the window, not the door (p. 308). At Chimkinichi a pupil of his saw the frame taken out so that the dead could be carried out through the window, though the usual way out was by the door and the stairs (p. 305).
A · The soul as a guest in the house

A / 02 The soul as a guest in the house Zelenin’s synthesis for the East Slavs (1991, § 132, pp. 345–346) records a vessel of water set beside the dying person and left on the table or the windowsill for forty days. During that time the soul is thought not yet to have gone to the other world, and some say it drinks the water; others say they saw the water stir as if the soul were bathing in it. At the moment of death a cloth or towel is hung out of the window, and the people give three explanations for it (the first section). In Belarus, on the night after the autumn memorial, a towel is hung out and pancakes and kutia are put on the window for the dead (p. 346, citing the archive of the Russian Geographical Society). Read together, these acts treat the soul as a person-like visitor who is washed, given water and a cloth, and sent on its way. The reading is Zelenin’s own summary of what people said, not a measurement of one community’s belief. The sources read for this edition do not tie the soul to breath or to bodily warmth, and the plate does not.

A / 03 Premonitions, and the problem of the motif Not established in the sources read Folklore motif; prevalence not established Folk narrative Signs of an approaching death (an animal’s behaviour, a knock in the house, an unusual shadow) are a standard topic in folklore handbooks, usually given as examples of a motif. A · Three claims and what was checked

Uncertainty register Three claims and what was checked That the mirror was covered to prevent the soul from being trapped. Field records document both this motive and the fear of doubling death (seeing the corpse reflected or looking into a mirror bringing a second death in the household; Tolstaya 1999, pp. 321–324). It is not a modern urban legend: the taboo on reflection is an established East Slavic ritual rule. That a body was carried out feet first. Zelenin reports it for northern Russians: the coffin was carried out open, feet first, so that the dead could not see the way back, and struck three times on the threshold of the house; in Olonets province it went out through the window (citing Barsov, vol. 1, p. 306), elsewhere through the back door or the cattle shed, and a woman with a bath-broom swept behind the procession (1991, pp. 348–349). Its age and wider distribution remain unverified. That the forty-day period is pre-Christian in origin. The scheme is documented in Orthodox liturgical handbooks; the claim that it continues an older pagan calendar is an interpretation, and a contested one.

A · Forty days in one district, and a dissenting encyclopedia

A / 07 Forty days in one district, and a dissenting encyclopedia One regional description gives the threshold a length. In Belozersk district, Vologda oblast, informants born between 1898 and 1935 told I. I. Razova that mirrors are covered for forty days; that coins are put on the window of the room where the body lies, then thrown into the grave to ‘buy’ the burial place; and that the door is not bolted for the whole forty days, because the dead are thought to come back until the fortieth day, sometimes as a bird at the window. A laundry beater across the doorway or rowan at the threshold keeps him out. The body is kept in the house for three days. Set beside the opened window of the first section, this is the opposite gesture: one practice lets the soul out, the other leaves the way in unbarred and then guards it. Whether these belong to one logic is the atlas’s question, not the informants’. The Great Russian Encyclopedia’s entry on East Slavic funerary rites, read only through a machine summary of the page, takes the other side of the plate’s claim about variants: it calls the rite on the whole uniform and stable, with local differences on the surface. The atlas keeps both statements, and notes that the first is a single district’s account of the 20th century, while the second is a synthesis across a much larger area. Here the household practice meets the church norm. The liturgical manual (Novaia Skrizhal, ch. XXIII § 2) anchors the fortieth-day commemoration strictly in scriptural typology: the forty days of Moses's fast on Sinai, the forty years in the wilderness, and the Ascension of Christ on the fortieth day, establishing this span as a time of liturgical intercession before the soul's private judgment. In village life, however, the forty days were lived as an empirical physical liminality: the soul was treated as an unadmitted guest traveling between home, grave and paths it walked in life, drinking from the cup on the window and eating vapor from the food until the final send-off (provody) on the fortieth day (Kremleva 1999, pp. 528–530; Zelenin 1991, p. 346).
B · Washing, and where the water goes

B / 01 Washing, and where the water goes Zelenin’s survey of East Slavic funeral rites puts the washing first: the body is washed in warm water and dressed in new clothes, and in many places this was once done while the dying person was still alive, because people believed one appears in the next world in the clothes in which one died. Since the moment of death is hard to catch, he suggests, washing the already dead became usual. A vessel of water stood beside the dying person for the soul to bathe in; some said they had seen the water stir. It stayed on the table or the windowsill for forty days, and some held that the soul drank from it (Zelenin 1991, pp. 345–346). For Russians he lists what happened to everything used in the last washing: the vessel, the washcloth, the straw on which the person died, sometimes the boards. These were carried to the field or beyond the village edge, and the vessel was usually smashed. In spring they could be thrown into a river in flood; if the master of the house had died they were often buried in the yard ‘so that the domovoi should not die out’ (citing Zavoiko, p. 91). The place where they lay inspired dread. Water that happened to be standing in the house at the moment of death was not drunk but poured out. A pregnant woman must not wash the dead, or her child will die. Ukrainians, he adds, poured the water where neither people nor animals walk, between two outbuildings or under a maize drier; that is a comparison, not Russian evidence (pp. 346, 349). The question of who washed the body and what they received is documented in systematic ethnographic surveys (Kremleva 1999, pp. 518–521; Baiburin 1993, pp. 102–108). Washing was entrusted almost exclusively to elderly women past childbearing age (myl'shchitsy or obmyval'shchitsy), often widows, or to unrelated neighbors. Close blood relatives—especially mothers, wives, and children—were strictly prohibited from washing the corpse: folk explanations held that a kin's tears would burn the dead, and the ritual aimed precisely at dismantling the physical ties between the deceased and the living household. Monetary wages were never paid: accepting money for handling the dead was regarded as a grave sin. Instead, the washers received ritual gifts 'for the remembrance of the soul' (na pomin dushi): towels, linen cuts, headscarves, the soap used in washing, or items of the deceased’s clothing. Barsov gives a compact Olonets version of the same sequence. As soon as people saw that someone was dying, a cup of water was set on the window; if the water stirred, they said ‘the little soul is washing’. For washing the body very old women were invited; he does not say whether they were kin or were paid. The dead person is usually washed with warm water on straw, opposite the chimney, from a clay vessel and rubbed twice with soap; in some places, Kondushi among them, a dead woman’s hair is cut and put in the coffin. The soap is then thrown into the river and the water poured out there, though sometimes both are kept: he says that sorcerers use the water to harm newly-weds, that a person made to drink it will waste away, and that the soap is used against fever (1872, pp. 302–303). The sorcery beliefs are reported, not observed; the passage names no informant.
B · Dress, and the ban on iron

B / 02 Dress, and the ban on iron Many old people sewed their own death clothes in advance and put them on before major feasts and in violent thunderstorms; the clothes were mostly white. If they were sewn for someone already dead, the seams were made with the needle pointing away from the sewer and toward the dead, in places with the left hand, and an old shirt that had to come off was torn. No outer garment was put on the dead; its place was taken by a savan, which could be a white shirt closed like a sack, or a length of cloth wrapped round and bound with a long strip. Modern or smart clothes were not used. Instead of boots, bast shoes or soft cloth footwear (kaligi); if the dead were already in boots, the iron nails were pulled out (Zelenin 1991, pp. 346–347). Cross and belt were strictly required; the cross was sometimes copper (silver was not allowed), and wooden ones were common. A woman never wore an apron; a man always had a hat, laid beside the body if the priest objected. A girl who died unmarried was dressed as for a wedding, with a ring on the middle finger of the right hand, gifts distributed by her kin as at a wedding and a wedding loaf on the coffin lid; a bachelor could be chosen as her ‘groom’ to walk behind the coffin, and something similar happened at a young man’s burial. Zelenin generalises these practices for the East Slavs; he does not date them or separate Russians from the others in every detail, so each belongs here to the region and group he names, where he names one. Barsov (1872, p. 303) says that in some places the dying person was asked beforehand what he wished to wear. For the Petrozavodsk, Olonets and Povenets districts he lists white boots or shoes sewn with one waxed thread, a shirt with a belt and a bone comb, a white balakhon with a sash over it, and a length of linen as a cover; in many Kargopol parishes a shroud was put on over a plain shirt. A cross on a woollen thread was always added, and for an Old Believer a rosary (chetki) as well. Clothes for the dead were sewn ‘inside out’, the needle pointing away from the sewer, which agrees with the seam rule above. His white boots or shoes differ from the bast shoes and soft footwear that Zelenin gives; the two describe different places and are not made to agree here.
B · The coffin and what went into it

B / 03 The coffin and what went into it Boards; formerly a hollowed trunk (koloda), still made so in parts of Olonets in Barsov’s time Recorded 1872 (Barsov) and 1927 (Zelenin); not dated further Container and bedding for the body The Russian word domovina and the older koloda name a coffin once made from a single trunk, with a small window and the head end often rounded; Zelenin says that by his time coffins were made of boards, fastened with wooden pegs, not iron nails, in places with bast. Pious people used to make their own coffins in advance, which was taken as a sign of long life, and scattered grain in them and gave grain to beggars (1991, p. 348). Shavings from the boards and dry leaves of the bath-broom were the usual bedding; the pillow was cut from the cloth of the burial clothes or from hay and stitched on three sides. Zelenin lists what was put in: bread, sometimes salt and butter, an egg at Easter, until recently a bottle of vodka for a man; copper coins tied in a kerchief at the belt, and coins in the grave. People read the coins differently: as payment for the burial place, as a way to keep the cattle from following the master (OR RGO, III, 1102), or, in the later reading, as a fare for crossing the fiery river or to pay off debts. For Belarusian forest areas he lists personal items, a pipe, a pouch, a child’s toy, a craftsman’s small tools, which he does not tie to Russians. The transition from handmade to purchased coffins is traced by late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century surveys (Kremleva 1999, pp. 521–523). In traditional villages, self-made hollowed trunks (kolody) or board coffins pegged without iron nails predominated well into the early twentieth century; elderly peasants commonly prepared their own coffins decades in advance, storing them in the granary or attic and filling them with rye grain as a sign of abundant life. In industrial settlements, railway towns, and suburban districts from the 1880s onward, carpenter workshops and trade stalls introduced mass-produced pine coffins, sold for 1 ruble 50 kopecks to 3–5 rubles for basic painted models. In remote northern and Siberian settlements, however, the handmade peg-joined coffin persisted throughout the Soviet era. Barsov (1872, pp. 302, 304–305) describes the Olonets coffin. Among the Suisar and Zaonezhye people it is a domovishche of dry boards, an oblong box; in some parishes, Syamozero and Badogi among them, openings with glass are cut at the sides opposite the dead person’s shoulders, elsewhere the glass is laid inside. In parts of the Ladeinoe Pole, Povenets and Kargopol districts (Lokshmoretsk parish is named) the coffin is a hollowed aspen or pine trunk, again with a small piece of glass. Shavings and chips from the coffin are thrown into a lake or taken to the forest. At Korela and elsewhere, leaves knocked off bath-brooms serve as bedding and fill the pillow. Gifts differ by place: bread in Nimenskoe parish (Kargopol district), pies at Brusno (Petrozavodsk district), a needle for women at Verkhovye (Olonets district), an egg for someone who dies at Easter, cut nails for the climb up the glass mountain. These are Barsov’s local notes and are not generalised.

B · Why the body is a difficult archive

Method Why the body is a difficult archive The body leaves no object. What survives is the description of the objects that surrounded it, written down later, often by outsiders. Ethnographers of the nineteenth century tended to record what they judged to be old. The date of a practice is therefore often the date of its recording, not of its origin.
B · Where the water goes, and what the soap keeps

B / 06 Where the water goes, and what the soap keeps Two Vologda descriptions give the disposal of washing water a purpose, and the purposes differ. For the Middle Sukhona, an overview page says the water was poured out in a special way, with a swing, at the corner of the house, in the yard and at crossroads, and that soap used in the washing was afterwards used to calm a restless family member or a restless animal, with a formula likening them to the dead who no longer kick. S. Adonyeva, speaking of the Vologda tradition recorded in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, says that the water, washcloth and soap are destroyed so that they cannot be used in harmful magic. In one account the leftovers are a remedy, in the other a danger. The Great Russian Encyclopedia, read only in extract, calls washing an obligatory part of the rite and notes that the washing, dressing and making of the coffin may be done by specially hired people. The atlas does not decide whether the two Vologda accounts describe two beliefs or one belief told twice; it keeps both and treats the plate’s earlier statement about a prohibition around disposal as the common ground. Academic ethnography (Kremleva 1999, pp. 519–520; Baiburin 1993, pp. 102–106) confirms that across European Russia the washing water ('dead water'), soap, and towels were treated as objects of acute ritual ambivalence. Because water absorbed the ritual impurity of physical death, it was poured into unfrequented spots (under the blank corner of the house, along fences, under nettles, or into a specially dug pit) where neither human foot nor livestock could tread. The soap, conversely, could be either buried to prevent sorcerers from using it for curses, placed into the coffin, or preserved as a potent remedy to wash ailments or calm restless beasts, likening them to the motionless dead.
C · The shape of the forty days

C / 01 The shape of the forty days The commemoration of the dead on the third, ninth and fortieth day after death is set out in Orthodox handbooks, and the reasons given there are theological and not calendrical. The Novaia Skrizhal’ (‘New Tablet’) of Archbishop Veniamin of Nizhny Novgorod (1739–1811), in its chapter of notes common to all funerals, § 2, gives more than one set. It cites Neophyte of Rhodes: the third day stands for Christ’s three days before the Resurrection, the ninth is a petition that the dead be numbered among the nine ranks of angels, and the fortieth echoes the forty days the people of Israel mourned Moses. It cites Simeon of Thessalonica, for whom the fortieth day recalls the Ascension, on the fortieth day after the Resurrection. And it adds its own reasoning: forty is a number Scripture sanctifies again and again, as in Moses’ fast, Elijah’s journey and Christ’s forty days with the apostles after the Resurrection. The same section sets aside one explanation. Some say, it reports, that the body changes its look on the third day, decays on the ninth and that the heart itself decays by the fortieth, but these reasons ‘do not always agree with experience’. The prayers are for the forgiveness of sins and for the soul’s place among the saints and the angels. The handbook does not mention the explanations recorded in villages, that the soul visits the house for three days or is examined on the ninth. For the fortieth day, Zelenin (1927, §§ 132, 136) records that the soul was thought not yet to have left before then, and that on that day it was ‘seen off’.

C / 04 Against the survival story Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century scholarship often read Russian funerary practice as a survival of pre-Christian religion with the Church laid over it. Zelenin (1927, § 154) writes that the bliny of Maslenitsa ‘undeniably’ show that the festival was once given to the commemoration of the dead: a reading of exactly this kind. A. K. Baiburin’s study of ritual in traditional culture, as the earlier edition summarised it and as this edition has not re-read it, treats ritual as a system of signs with its own internal logic, not as a fossil of an earlier belief, and holds that what a rite ‘originally meant’ is usually not recoverable from the surviving evidence. This atlas therefore marks origin claims as interpretations. The forty-day cycle is documented as Christian. Whether some households also understood it as an older calendar is a question the sources used here cannot settle.

C · The lament: spontaneous, and rehearsed

C / 07 The lament: spontaneous, and rehearsed Lamenting is the part of the ritual most often described as raw feeling. Barsov, publishing in 1872, called the laments immediate outpourings of the thoughts and feelings that loss provokes. Elena Yugai, working from interviews in several districts of Vologda Oblast with women mostly born in the 1920s–1940s, reports two kinds of lamenter in their stories: a paid specialist, and a bereaved relative who begins to lament without having planned to. The second is the one the stories are about. The same women also describe preparing: practising alone in remote places, listening closely to experienced lamenters, sometimes learning from an old woman for payment. Yugai says this training had to be kept out of sight, since the appearance of spontaneity and personal involvement belonged to the performance, and that grief itself is spoken of as the teacher. On function she reads the laments as ritual texts with a melody that imitates weeping, addressed to the dead. At a funeral they help move the deceased into the status of an ancestor, at a commemoration they secure the protection of dead relatives, and they limit the grief of widows and orphans. This is an interpretation by one researcher, from Vologda material only, and it sets itself against both Barsov’s romantic reading and the women’s own account. The atlas keeps both: what the women say they do, and what the researcher says the rite does.
C · What the handbook says about wailing

C / 08 What the handbook says about wailing The same Novaia Skrizhal’ (ch. XX, § 15, ‘The use of the funeral lament’) is not friendly to wailing. It says it was noticed long ago that women who, tormented by unreasoning despair, in torn clothes and with loose hair, cry out at the death of those close to them do not soften the pain but increase it and rouse others to the same weeping and praise of the dead. It recalls that the Council of Carthage forbade bishops to add their own mournful chants or eulogies to the prayers fixed by councils, and readers to use ‘wedding exclamations’ in place of church singing. The Church nevertheless allowed some mournful hymns of its own, the handbook says, to turn attention to death and the life to come, and it names the troparion sung at the end of the rite, which speaks as if with the dead person’s voice and calls friends and kin to weeping. The passage is about ancient women’s wailing in general and about clerics who improvised; it does not name Russian peasant laments, and the atlas does not claim it was aimed at them. It does show that a handbook current in Russia from 1803 treats set church lament as acceptable and improvised lament as a fault.

D / 01 The hot dinner On the day of burial everyone who came was fed. Zelenin’s survey of East Slavic ethnography (1927; 1991 edition, § 136, pp. 356–357) explains the name of the ‘hot dinner’ (Russian goriachii, Belarusian garachyi): hot bread was always served, broken by hand and not cut with a knife, so that steam would rise. The dead were thought to need food like the living, and to feed in part on the steam from it. Ukrainians broke fresh bread in two and put it on the windowsill so that the hot steam would reach the dead. While the dead person was still in the house they were given bliny: the first, still hot and sometimes smeared with honey, was put on the bench at the head, on the windowsill or on the shelf of icons. At the funeral and the wakes a separate place was laid for the dead, either at the common table or at a special table in the corner under the icons, and the first spoonful of any dish and the first glass of water were poured out at the corner of the table for them. The usual dishes were kutia (also kolivo, kanun), boiled barley or wheat in honey diluted with water, then bliny, honey kisel, fried eggs and porridge; the main drink was beer or braga sweetened with honey. In the Russian North, guests were given a wooden spoon after dinner in memory of the dead. Zelenin merges Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian material and cites the archive of the Russian Geographical Society by volume and number; those files were not seen, and he gives no dates. The sequence of the meal was strictly regimented across Russian provinces (Kremleva 1999, pp. 526–527; Baiburin 1993, pp. 110–112). It began with three spoonfuls of kutia (kanun, kolivo), which every guest had to taste before any other food. Knives and forks were strictly banned as piercing instruments that could harm the unseen guest; only wooden spoons were used. After kutia came hot cabbage soup (shchi) or fish broth (ukha) served with hot bread, then porridge or noodles, followed by bliny with honey. The meal ended with thick oat or berry kisel; drinking the kisel was the ritual signal for diners to rise, thank the hosts, and disperse.

D · Kutia, and the ambiguity of grain

D / 04 Kutia, and the ambiguity of grain Kutya is boiled grain sweetened with honey, and in its church form, kolivo, it is brought to the memorial service and blessed. The Novaia Skrizhal’ (1803, ch. XXIII, § 3) names boiled wheat with honey and gives the reading: the wheat that dies in the ground and then bears fruit stands for the resurrection of the dead, and the honey for the sweet, blessed life that awaits the righteous in the Kingdom of Heaven. It adds Simeon of Thessalonica’s reading of the seeds offered in the same way. What ethnographic surveys show is that the funeral table was neither a purely canonical rite nor a mere 'pagan survival' (Baiburin 1993, pp. 110–115; Kremleva 1999, pp. 526–529). Church blessing of kolivo and the domestic serving of hot steam and honeyed grain functioned as interlocking parts of one commemorative dialogue. While theological manuals emphasised spiritual resurrection through the grain metaphor, peasant practice treated the meal as a reciprocal feeding that satisfied the dead, bound the community, and ensured the soul's peaceful departure without lingering to haunt the homestead.
D · Forty days, and the table for the way home

D / 05 Forty days, and the table for the way home Zelenin (1927, § 136) ties several dishes to the dead person’s journey. In south Russian practice a ‘ladder’ (lesenka) was baked for the fortieth day, an oblong flat cake with 3, 24 or 40 cross-stripes like the steps of a stair, taken as the dead person’s climb to heaven. It was set on a bench at the gate, a requiem was sung, and the cake was then eaten with honey. Some people on that day ate bliny at the nearest crossroads, which was meant to keep the dead from finding the way home. The fortieth day is the ‘seeing off’ of the soul, and in the North a special bed was made up for the dead in the corner under the icons on the eve, so that they would rest before the long road. Zelenin adds three items that are not Russian and are kept here as comparison. In Volhynia a bonfire was lit at the cemetery on the spring day for the dead and a common dinner cooked for all present. Belarusians on the ‘grandfathers’ days (dziady), the Saturdays before Maslenitsa and before St Demetrius’s day, set aside a little of each dish in a bowl by the window and poured out the first spoonful and glass with the words ‘Grandfather, come to dinner!’. Grain was scattered for birds on graves and sometimes at crossroads, which he tentatively links to the widespread idea of the soul as a bird; he adds that this is now done mainly for the ‘unclean’ dead. The days of the calendar are on plate U. Barsov’s Olonets passages put some of these items in named districts. At the funeral dinner in Ladeinopol district an empty place is left at the table in the front corner, a spoon is laid under the tablecloth and bread on the cloth (1872, p. 307). On the fortieth day the relatives go out of the house to meet the priest, fully believing that the dead person is coming with him; in Brusnoe (Petrozavodsk district) a bed is made up beside the priest’s, if he arrives on the eve, for the unseen guest, and at the dinner a separate empty place with its own setting is left in the front corner while the dead person’s favourite dish is named (p. 308; the page gives no locality for the last detail). In Ladeinopol district a table with cutlery and dishes is also set on the stove for the dead, who after forty days in a cold country is said to have grown chilled and needs to warm himself (p. 309). These are local practices, and Barsov does not say how widespread any of them was.
D · Why a Ukrainian photograph is here

Outside Russia Why a Ukrainian photograph is here The atlas treats ‘Russian’ as a language, a state tradition and a set of institutions, not as a synonym for East Slavic. Where a photograph documents a Ukrainian or Belarusian practice, it is labelled as such. The meal at the grave is widely attested across the region, which makes it exactly the kind of practice that gets mislabelled as ‘Russian’ by default.
D · When the table has to wait

Lent When the table has to wait The table follows the church calendar. A reference page on the parental Saturdays states that when someone died before or during Great Lent, the commemorations on the third, ninth and fortieth days were not held in mid-week, when there is no full Liturgy, but moved to the nearest Saturday. The same page says that church rules do not regulate the memorial meal at all and offers a single guideline, moderation. The meal is therefore a custom set inside a calendar, not a rite with its own canon; the household negotiates between the two. The page names no author and describes the rule in the past tense, so the atlas uses it as a statement of the rule, not as evidence of how many households followed it.

E / 01 Zelenin’s ‘pledged’ dead In 1916 D. K. Zelenin published a study of those who die an unnatural death — by suicide, accident, murder, drowning, or before their time — and of the rusalki. His term for them, zalozhnye pokoiniki, is usually translated as ‘pledged’ or ‘unclean’ dead: those whose death was not completed within the order of things. Zelenin argued that such dead were buried apart, outside the cemetery or at its edge, in ravines, fields or at crossroads, and that they were believed to remain active — to walk, to appear, to harm. The book is a work of synthesis and it is also a work of its time, assembled from scattered reports into a system that no single informant would have recognised.

E / 02 The dispute Later scholarship has treated Zelenin’s category with caution. The reports he gathered come from different provinces, different decades and different genres — legend, memorate, custom, ecclesiastical prohibition — and the boundary between ‘unclean’ and ‘clean’ death was drawn differently from place to place. Whether the rusalka is a development of the unclean dead, as Zelenin proposed, remains an interpretation rather than a finding. The atlas therefore presents zalozhnye as a scholarly construction built on real reports, not as a folk taxonomy that everyone shared. The reports are evidence. The category is an argument.
E · Invited, fed and sent off: the dead on memorial days

E / THE ORDINARY DEAD Invited, fed and sent off: the dead on memorial days Svetlana Tolstaya’s 2024 article draws on published and archive collections of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and on field recordings made by her and her colleagues in Polesie (the Belarus–Ukraine borderland) in the 1960s–80s and in the Russian North and the Carpathians in the 1990s. It describes contact between the living and the dead as regulated by time, place and means, and as largely one-sided: the living perform actions, the dead are invisible and are known only by indirect signs, sounds and footprints (pp. 6–7). Her material is pan-Slavic, so the places are given below, and the Belarusian, Serbian and Slovene items are comparisons, not evidence about Russians. For the East Slavs she lists how the dead were called on memorial days: at the gate, porch, window or door, with treats, in a high-pitched voice. A place was left at the table with a glass; a little of each dish was put aside or poured on a plate or under the table; food stayed on the table overnight; a towel was hung out so they could wash their hands; doors were not shut at night; clothes were hung in the yard for them (Slavic Antiquities, vol. 4, pp. 269–272, and her own field archive). Where the souls were not fed they were said to weep that they were hungry (vol. 2, p. 43). In Mogilev province, Belarus, people prepared a bath for the dead and, after the meal, poured water from the table to the door and told them to fly back to their place (Shein 1890, pp. 597, 609). In Polesie, on the day after the funeral, relatives took food from the memorial meal to the grave, which was called ‘waking the dead’ (field archive). In the Russian North, at the wake on the fortieth day, small children were carried round the table and asked whether they could see their father, uncle or aunt (Barsov 1997, p. 251) (pp. 6–7). The main channel she names is dreams. The dead come to complain that the wrong clothes were put in the coffin, or that they are hungry because no memorial meal was held, or that the grave is full of water because the living wept too much, and the living respond: in one pan-Slavic account they dug up the grave to see whether the coffin was really floating (p. 8). Greetings and news for the dead could be passed in the text of a lament, which she says was common in the Russian North (Barsov 1997). She argues that this whole pattern does not sit comfortably with the usual notion of an ‘ancestor cult’: the dead are both honoured and feared, and the living feel dependent on them and anxious to keep the boundary between the two worlds (abstract, p. 1). She is one scholar, writing for a mixed Slavic sample. Barsov records signs by which the living told whether the dead had come to a fortieth-day meal. In Samozero parish, where a table with dishes is set on the stove, they look afterwards to see whether the spoon is wet or dry. In some places in Ladeinopol district someone climbs onto the stove beforehand and looks at the table through a horse collar; a footnote from a correspondent has a close relative do this in a fur coat, looking through a sieve, and calls a sight of the dead a good sign. At Ezhessel small children are carried round the table and asked whether they see father, uncle or aunt, and if they repeat the last words, they see the unseen guest; if a bed was made up the night before, it is examined next day for creases (1872, p. 310). The next passage is a comparison, and Barsov labels it as such: among the Mordvins of two districts of Penza province, the family spreads a featherbed with the dead man’s favourite clothes in the front corner and waits for him; when he does not appear, at dawn one of his favourites goes to the grave, calls him, comes back in his likeness, bows on all sides and sits at the table, and old women ask him with deep bows whether life is good in the next world (pp. 310–311). This is a Mordvin rite, not a Russian one. The package that suggested the passage left its locality unmarked; the page does not. In the Russian North, field studies among Pechora Old Believers in Ust-Tsilma document how the recently dead (novoprestavlennyi) is kept apart from the general collective of ancestors (roditeli) (Dronova 2024, pp. 201–204). For the first forty days, the deceased is perceived as precarious, fragile and directly dependent on living kin for clothing, prayers and food. Dreams during these weeks are read as urgent demands: an informant describes a father appearing barefoot in a dream because winter boots were omitted from his coffin, prompting the family to immediately give boots to an elderly neighbour 'for his soul'; other dreams report the dead being drenched when kin weep too excessively. Once the fortieth-day 'seeing-off' (provody) is accomplished and commemorated after the first year, the dead person merges into the quiet, benevolent body of 'parents', remembered on seasonal Saturdays and ceasing to disturb the household in dreams.
E · Case notes, without the case

E / 03 Case notes, without the case Ethnographic report, legend, memorate 19th–early 20th c. No individual narrative is quoted here The reports share a structure: a death that violates expectation, a burial that violates place, and a subsequent sighting or disturbance. The disturbance is usually resolved by a ritual action — moving the body, reading a prayer, driving a stake, calling the priest — and the resolution tells us more about the living than about the dead. No narrative is reproduced verbatim in this atlas. The genre is highly variable, the published texts are often retold rather than transcribed, and a single vivid quotation would misrepresent the record as more uniform than it is.
E · What the category was for

E / 04 What the category was for The unclean dead mark the limits of the community’s obligation. They are the people for whom the full ritual was not, or could not be, performed — and the fear they provoke is the fear of an obligation left unpaid. In this reading the revenant is less a monster than an unpaid debt with a voice. That reading is the atlas’s interpretation, offered as such. It does not require the dead to be real; it requires the living to have accounts.

Caution No vampires here Russian and Ukrainian records do contain stories of the dead who rise and feed, and the word upyr’ is attested. It is a different figure from the nineteenth-century literary vampire, and the atlas does not read the one through the other. The atlas avoids the vocabulary of horror. ‘Returning’ is a social event in these sources, not a genre.
A bad death is the one that leaves something owing, not the one that hurts most. Editorial note
E · Where the category began: Vyatka, 1909

E / 07 Where the category began: Vyatka, 1909 In the preface read here, Zelenin says the study did not start in a Russian village. In the summer of 1909 he surveyed the Besermyans, a small people of Vyatka province, and noted a rite he calls kuyas’kon: an offering thrown with contempt, fear and hatred to people who had died young by unnatural death, among them a miller’s wife killed in a fall from a tree, miscarried infants and murdered families of an unknown people. Seeking the same beliefs among Russians and their neighbours led him to an article of 1911 in Zhivaya starina on the cult of those dead by unnatural death among Russians and Finns, and then to the book of 1916 (Petrograd, A. V. Orlov, 328 pages). The origin matters for the plate’s dispute. The category of the ‘pledged’ dead was assembled in the first place from a non-Russian rite and extended to Russian reports, which, in the atlas’s reading, adds a reason for the caution recorded above. Only the preface was read, in a modern reissue whose editing differs from the first edition, so the atlas does not judge how far Zelenin’s extension holds.

F / 01 The decree of 1723 By a decree of Peter I dated 10 October 1723, burial in towns was restricted, with an exception for notable persons, because the churchyards at churches and monasteries had become overcrowded. Pravenc reports that the same decree ordered raised tombs levelled and relief images on shrines replaced with painted ones. A nineteenth-century account by N. P. Rozanov gives the decree this way: only ‘notable persons’ could be buried at churches in Moscow and other towns, and the rest were to go to monasteries and parish churches outside the town. He assigns the order to lower tombstones to ground level, with the inscriptions on top, to an earlier decree of 12 April 1722, and does not mention tombs or relief images in the 1723 text. One academic article dates the burial decree 16 October, not 10 October. The atlas keeps 10 October as Pravenc and Rozanov give it and treats the tombstone order as unsettled. The measure did not last. Rozanov says the decree was not carried out because Peter died in January 1725, and that the old custom of burying at the parish churches stayed as it was under his successors. The change came in 1771, when plague struck Moscow. Rozanov names a Senate decree of 24 March 1771 that set aside special places outside the town for those who died of the disease, and one of 1 November 1771 ordering that burials at town churches stop and that cemeteries be laid out outside the towns. The article on Siberia dates a Senate decree of the same kind to 24 December 1771, and the atlas does not reconcile the dates. Vagankovo was founded in that year to receive the plague dead. The municipal note says the first burials there were unnamed Muscovites and gives no figure for the dead; popular accounts vary widely, and none is used here. Ecclesiastical canon and folk practice converged strictly on the orientation of the grave (Belova and Levkievskaya 2004, pp. 263–265). Across Orthodox parishes, the body was laid on its back, head to the west and feet to the east, looking toward the east where Christ is expected to appear at the Second Coming. The placement of the cross varied: in general parish practice it was erected at the foot of the grave so that the rising dead could behold the crucifix and embrace it on the day of resurrection; among many Old Believer communities and in northern regions, it was set at the head to shelter the departed under the sign of the cross. Church legislation from the early eighteenth century (Holy Synod decrees of 1707, 1722 and 1723) repeatedly banned the erection of enclosed wooden miniature houses (domoviny) and roofed shrines over graves as pagan survivals, commanding simple flat crosses instead.

F / 02 Out of the town, 1771–72 Rozanov’s own wording for the Senate decree of 1 November 1771 is that burial at churches in towns should stop and that cemeteries be laid out outside the town on common grazing land, with small wooden churches built on them at first, at the town’s expense; places where plague victims were already buried were not to be dug up. In Moscow the cemeteries and their wooden churches were set up under the architect Bazhanov and Brigadier Durnov, who handed the consistory a register of six new churches on 31 December 1772. Vagankovo’s church of St John the Merciful is on that register. Consecration followed soon, he says, without a date in the part read. He lists six cemeteries made after the plague: Dorogomilovskoe, Vagankovskoe, Miusskoe, Pyatnitskoe, Kalitnikovskoe and Danilovskoe. They stayed unarranged for years. Rozanov writes that the better-off were mostly buried in monasteries, that burial at the new cemeteries brought the clergy little income, and that the clergy received no money from the treasury. Of the Moscow monasteries only Spaso-Andronikov, Novospassky, Donskoy and Novodevichy kept burying. The sources read say nothing about walls, plans, registers or fees.
F · The roof over the cross

F / 03 The roof over the cross The golubets — a cross sheltered by a small gabled roof, sometimes enclosed as a little house — is a grave form that can still be seen in Russian cemeteries. The word had a second meaning, a built-in box beside the stove in a peasant house. The roof protects the wood; it also makes the cross into a building, and the grave into a dwelling. Architectural and ethnographical surveys across the Russian North (Permilovskaya 2013, pp. 312–330; Belova and Levkievskaya 2004, pp. 264–266) document the roofed cross (krest-golubets) not as an isolated oddity, but as an established micro-architectural tradition across the Mezen, Pinega, Pechora, and White Sea Pomor basins, as well as in remote Siberian settlements. In these regions, the timber roof—complete with miniature gabled rafters (pričeliny) and carved bargeboards—directly mirrored the roof of the northern log izba. The grave was conceived in peasant culture as the 'eternal house' (vechnoe zhilishche), and the roof sheltered both the wood against harsh Arctic snow and the small carved or painted icon set in the kiyot under the gable. Preserved predominantly by Old Believers who defied Synodal bans, the form continued in active use well into the mid-twentieth century. Barsov saw small houses with a roof and windows over some graves in his childhood, and in Novgorod province, in Cherepovets district, for example at Prechistaya in Andoga (1872, p. 307). The same page records that those who took part in a burial touched the stove with a hand on coming home. His note is one district; it does not give the word golubets and does not say how common the houses were.

F / 04 Novodevichy Cemetery, Moscow Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow grew up around the convent founded in the sixteenth century, as the traditional burial place of the church and noble elite of Moscow, and in the nineteenth century of the intelligentsia and merchants. A new cemetery was opened south of the convent wall in 1898, enclosed in 1898–1904 and extended in 1949. An encyclopedia entry, seen only as a search excerpt, names it as the burial place of well-known Soviet state, party and military figures, scholars, writers and actors. Rozanov, writing of the 1770s–80s, names Novodevichy among the four Moscow monasteries (with Spaso-Andronikov, Novospassky and Donskoy) where burial continued after the new cemeteries were opened. Two examples recorded in the photographs used by this atlas: the grave of Ilya Ilf, and a double monument for the writer A. N. Stepanov and his wife, designed — according to the photographer’s description — as two ships on a dark sea. The atlas repeats that description as a description, not as a documented intention of the family.

Unverified Portraits on stone Photographic portraits set into headstones are a familiar feature of late-Soviet and post-Soviet cemeteries. The atlas has not found a scholarly source for their chronology and does not date them here. The same caution applies to the enamel photograph, the plastic wreath and the metal fence: visible everywhere, documented in the sources used here almost nowhere.
F · Tobolsk: closed ground, an old man’s request, two infants

F / 11 Tobolsk: closed ground, an old man’s request, two infants The law of the cemetery reached Siberia as paperwork. A Senate decree of 24 December 1771 banned burial at town parish churches and called for new ground outside the town; the Tobolsk consistory applied it to villages of its eparchy, and in 1783 the parish of Abalak was moved to Preobrazhenskoye while the old church complex became a monastery. Lay burial at Abalak stopped. In August 1815, though, a peasant of Abalak volost, Alexey Vakhrushev, was buried inside the monastery enclosure after a service by a priest of the Preobrazhenskaya church, without the knowledge of the local authorities. The abbot said the elderly man, ill with tuberculosis and asthma, had asked for it before he died. The gubernia board wanted exhumation; more than twenty days had passed, and sanitary risk prevented it. A Synod decree of 12 April 1833 later allowed burial in closed cemeteries in exceptional cases, such as priests and large donors, and in 1912–13 the consistory reviewed 19 petitions for burial within church or monastery enclosures and refused one. The law also had a smaller edge. Stillborn and unbaptized children could lie in general cemeteries but without rites or commemoration. At the abandoned village of Yarkova, in the Tobolsk district, archaeologists in 2015 opened a 50 m² trench in a garden plot beside a cliff and found two children’s burials of the mid-nineteenth to early twentieth century, in logs, shallow, with twisted cords and some factory cloth. With no other graves nearby, the authors read it as a household plot for unbaptized infants. That is their reading, from two burials, and the sources do not say which of two long-settled families used it.
G · Barsov’s volumes: who laments for whom

G / 01 Barsov’s volumes: who laments for whom The first volume of E. V. Barsov’s Prichitaniia Severnogo kraia (Moscow, 1872) arranges its funeral laments by the relationship between the dead person and the one who laments: a widow for her husband comes first (printed p. 1), then a daughter for her father and for her mother, laments for a wife, a son, a daughter, a goddaughter, a brother, a sister, uncles and cousins, and then for the drowned (p. 252), for a drunkard (p. 271), for a village elder, a clerk and a priest (p. 293). The headings and page numbers are taken from the contents page of the Internet Archive scan, as machine-read OCR (the first page, the drowned, the drunkard and the priest were read again in the Internet Archive text on 16 November 2026 and match), and have not been collated with a paper copy. In the introduction Barsov separates the professional lamenter from the household in mourning: the people, he writes, produce figures who long remain carriers of the old funeral lament, known as voplenitsy; he also notes that whole villages sometimes gather to pay the dead their last duty (pp. II–III). A lament has no fixed text of the kind an epic song has. Kuznetsova and Kovyrshina (Petrozavodsk, 2000) describe a local ‘school’ of lamenters as a shared stock of obligatory motifs, formulas, compositional patterns and melodies, learned informally from childhood by girls who watched village weddings and acted them out in play. Their example is from Vyrozero in the Zaonezhye: an ordinary performer’s wedding lament runs to some 40–50 lines, Fedosova’s lament at the handclasp to 1,074. That figure belongs to a wedding lament, not a funeral one; it shows how far a single performer could lengthen a text by improvising between formulas.
G · A funeral day in laments, as Vologda performers describe it

G / VOLOGDA A funeral day in laments, as Vologda performers describe it Elena Iugai’s study draws on funeral laments of the eastern part of Vologda province, published by B. Efimenkova (1980) and by Iugai herself (2011), and begins with a warning: the Olonets laments of Barsov’s volumes are not representative of all Russian laments, because his informants Fedosova, Bogdanova and Pashkova were not ordinary lament-singers, their texts being very long and rich; a fair picture needs a large corpus of smaller texts, such as those from the Novgorod region (Berdyaeva 2015) and the South Urals (Rozhkova and Moiseeva 2008) (p. 166). She says that in pre-revolutionary Russia laments were an obligatory part of the funeral, with different types for different stages, and that the genre has since lost that role (p. 167). The performers’ own names for laments mark moments: ‘when he is lying on the bench’, ‘when they carry the coffin’, ‘in the cemetery’, the last covering laments at the digging of the grave, at the anniversary and on visits to the cemetery on Trinity Saturday. On the day of burial, as she describes it, relatives lament in the house of the dead while guests lament on their way to it. The text narrates a search: the performer wakes, washes, looks for the dead person in the yard and the house, finds him in the red corner and reproaches his silence. When the helpers close the coffin she laments again, asking them not to. The full ‘parting in the house’ can run to hundreds of lines. On the way to the cemetery the dead says farewell to the house, the street, the village, the forests and the whole world; at the cemetery the lament soothes the dead, whose relatives are waiting for him; a last lament is sung on the way back (pp. 167–168). Informants separate these from commemoration laments, which are more symbolic, less improvised and closer to lyrical songs, and which can be sung within the first 39 days (on the ninth or twentieth), on the fortieth day, at the anniversary, on feast days or on any day. The soul is thought to come to the commemoration feast: in some Vologda villages a table is laid for the souls and a clean towel hung out for them to wash their hands, and a lament invites them. In the west of the province there is a lament inviting the dead to the bath; in the east the bath is prepared but no lament belongs to it. Today, she says, a performer often knows only one short lament, built from the traditional formulas, and uses it both at funerals and at commemorations (pp. 168–169). This is one author’s description of one region; it does not say how widely the same sequence held elsewhere. Barsov’s own note on the funeral dinner shows the laments as an order of performance. In the Olonets passage that puts the dead person’s table on the stove (Ladeinopol district), the lamenters begin at the first dish, first lamenting to the priest and the clergy, then to relatives, neighbours and outsiders present; they walk through the house, bow to the four corners and lament at every place where the dead person sat, lay and walked, then go out to the barn, the yard and, if near, the fields. The sequence repeats after the second and third dishes, the lamenters change after each, and the priest is seen off with tears in the belief that the dead goes back to the cemetery with him (1872, p. 309). Barsov’s introduction also records what church and state made of lamenting. It quotes the Stoglav Council of 1551, which complained that on Trinity Saturday men and women at the graves wept with great shouting and, when buffoons and musicians began to play, stopped weeping to dance and sing ‘satanic songs’, and told priests to turn their flocks from these ‘pagan customs’ (ch. 4, q. 23); and a decree of 1715 in which Peter I, on the death of Tsaritsa Marfa Matveevna, ordered that no one should give such indecent howling over her or over any other dead person. Barsov says the decree touched the Westernised upper layer and had no influence on the mass of the people, and adds that Peter’s own coffin was lamented in a folk lament (pp. VIII–IX). Both are quoted at second hand, and ‘pagan’ is the Council’s word, not a finding.

G / 02 Occasions, not a score Funeral lament (prichitanie) Olonets province, published 1872 Performed, formulaic, address in the second person Barsov’s introduction ties laments to successive occasions: the moment of dying, the burial, and later visits when the mourner speaks to the dead and invites them back into the house. The passage ranges over several pages (about pp. V–XVI) and the individual pages have not been collated. The six-part movement of address, question about the road, complaint, self-reproach, description of the grave and farewell, which an earlier version of this plate presented ‘after Barsov’, is the atlas’s own working schema. It was not checked against the printed laments and is withdrawn as a statement about Barsov’s texts.

G / 03 The second person Collation of the primary lament corpus (Barsov 1872, part I; Kuznetsova and Kovyrshina 2000, pp. 153–160) confirms that Russian funerary language keeps the dead strictly in the second person singular (ty) and in the present tense for the entire duration of the rites. The performer invokes the deceased through kin epithets—'my master', 'my born one', 'my bright light' (sudaruška ty moi, svet-nadeža ty moia)—and poses continuous rhetorical questions ('To whom do you leave us?', 'Whither are you preparing to go?') that demand an answer. Ordinary euphemisms for death (ušel—'he has gone'; ne stalo—'he is no more') are suspended: the lament is constructed as an intense dramatic dialogue that refuses to acknowledge the silence of the corpse until the grave is filled. Third-person grammatical forms occur only when the lamenter breaks the direct address to instruct gravediggers, remonstrate with onlookers, or petition God.

G · Fedosova, and the question of the author

The performer Fedosova, and the question of the author Most of the laments in Barsov’s volumes were recorded from one woman, Irina Andreevna Fedosova (1827–1899), a lamenter from the Zaonezhye north of Lake Onega; a few were added later from her by O. Kh. Agreneva-Slavianskaia. Kuznetsova and Kovyrshina place her birth in a village of the Vyrozero district (née Yulina) and her later life at Kuzarand; her melodies were noted between 1886 and 1895 by Agreneva-Slavianskaia, S. G. Rybakov and N. A. Rimsky-Korsakov, and a phonograph recording of 1896 by Yu. I. Blok was transcribed and published much later. Reference works disagree on her birth year, 1827 or 1831, and this atlas follows the 1827 given in the scholarly articles read. The consequence for the plate is concrete. A genre described above as formulaic and communal reaches us largely through a single, exceptionally skilled voice, recorded by outsiders, in a setting that was not a funeral. Philologists have debated how much of the printed text is the tradition and how much is the performer. The sources read here do not allow the atlas to settle that, and it does not. Fedosova was not the only named voice. In the register of performers that closes the first volume, Barsov lists five women, and the lament printed there as No. XI comes from a peasant woman of the village of Tverdilovo, Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province, Klavdiya Momokova, who by his account learned to lament in her own village while still unmarried and was living in Moscow when he wrote. Another, Anna Perventseva, was a priest’s daughter who learned at the churchyard on Sundays and feast days; a third, Marya Fedorova of Kargopol, a deacon’s daughter, learned from an old lamenter who had taken shelter in her parents’ house. The portraits are Barsov’s own, selective and at times unfriendly, and give no recording dates; they show that the collection rests on named women of different standing, not on an anonymous “people”.

H / 01 What the Church says The handbook Novaia Skrizhal’ (1803) gives the Church’s reasons for commemorating the dead on the third, ninth and fortieth days, and Simeon of Thessalonica, whom it quotes, adds a yearly commemoration by the relatives. The ninth day asks that the dead be counted among the nine angelic ranks and in the company of the saints; the fortieth is tied by Simeon to the Ascension, so that the dead may be raised to meet the Judge. Neophyte of Rhodes ties it to Israel’s mourning for Moses, and the handbook itself points to the number forty in Scripture. Only chapter XXIII §§ 2–3 were read; the funeral service is not quoted here. The Church’s language about the state between death and the resurrection is restrained in the passages read. That restraint is an editorial reading, not a quotation. Where popular literature supplies a detailed itinerary (where the soul goes on which day, what it sees), the atlas marks it as devotional or folk elaboration, not as doctrine. A profound divide between canonical dogma and vernacular belief governed the fate of early dead and unbaptised children (Sedakova 2020, pp. 51–58; Dronova 2024, pp. 203–205). In Orthodox canonical theology, infants who died unbaptised bore no personal sins and thus endured no active torment in Gehenna, but being uncleansed of ancestral sin, they could not receive church burial, liturgical commemoration (panikhida), or enter into the beatific vision. In vernacular practice, this exclusion generated profound anxiety: unbaptised infants were buried outside sacred ground—beneath house eaves (so rainwater might symbolically wash them), under thresholds, or along fence boundaries—and popular eschatological tales envisioned them wandering in a dark borderland as unquiet souls (kukiata, poterchata) pleading for a cross. Baptised children, conversely, were celebrated in folk faith as sinless 'angels' dwelling immediately in the celestial gardens of Eden; loud maternal wailing over them was formally discouraged lest excessive tears 'soak their angelic wings' in Paradise.

H / 02 Reading the icon The Last Judgment icon is a diagram as much as a painting. What the reproduction shows: a title across the top and long columns of text down both sides; Christ enthroned in glory with saints on either side; scales near the centre; a red river of fire on the right ending in a monstrous mouth; a winding band with labelled stations; a gate with the righteous at the lower left; and a row of small compartments of torment along the bottom, each with a caption. The small lettering could not be read in this reproduction, so no inscription is quoted and no social type is assigned to any compartment. The Commons description of the icon calls it typical of mid-to-late eighteenth-century iconography and says it was influenced by printed engravings. The atlas reads the text columns and captioned compartments as page-like in that sense. Who made the icon, for whom, and in what milieu is not stated in the description; an earlier version spoke of an urban artisan milieu and of viewers who read, and both statements are withdrawn.

H · Theology is not a mood

Caution Theology is not a mood The icon’s punishments are evidence of a moral taxonomy, so the atlas does not use them as atmosphere or decoration. Where a popular belief contradicts or exceeds the Church’s formulation, the atlas says so rather than harmonising them.
H · A narrative that is not a dogma

The toll-houses A narrative that is not a dogma The best-known popular itinerary of the soul in Russia comes from one text: the vision of Theodora in the Life of St Basil the New. In it the dead woman appears to Basil’s disciple Gregory and describes how angels escorted her through a series of trials, at which evil spirits tried to claim her soul for its sins. According to the Orthodox Encyclopedia, as cited in a Russian theological article, the Life was written in Constantinople in the second half of the tenth century and exists in several redactions. The same article states that the toll-house narrative became widely accepted but never acquired the status of a binding dogma of the Church, and reads its images as parable-like language, not as literal topography. The atlas takes the distinction from that article: the narrative is documented as hagiography and widely received; its status as doctrine is disputed in the very source that defends it. The article was read, not the Life itself, so no list of the trials is given here.

I / 01 1771: the pit The Moscow plague of 1771 killed many thousands of people; the municipal note used here gives no total. The dead were buried outside the city, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo received, first of all, unnamed people. The historical account of the cemetery begins with a number it cannot disaggregate. Mass death produces this kind of record: a pit, a total, a name for the place, no names for the people. The atlas does not illustrate the pit. It prints the fact of it. Archival demographic studies of the 1770–1772 Moscow plague estimate total mortality between 50,000 and 100,000 victims, precipitating a permanent transformation of Russian burial geography. The Senate decrees of 24 March and 1 November 1771 marked the first absolute civil prohibition against churchyard interments in Russian cities. To prevent pestilence, the municipal administration mandated the creation of dedicated burial grounds beyond the Kamer-Kollezhsky customs rampart—founding Vagankovo, Danilovskoe, Miusskoe, and Rogozhskoe as mass sanitary burial tracts where thousands of plague dead were interred in common lime-dusted trenches.

I / 02 The unknown soldier The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Kremlin wall was opened on 8 May 1967. The monument was designed by the architects Dmitrii Burdin, Vladimir Klimov and Iurii Rabaev, with the sculptor Nikolai Tomskii; the remains had been brought from a mass grave outside Moscow. The eternal flame was lit at the opening and has been maintained since. The unknown soldier is a very specific solution to a problem of scale: it converts an unmanageable number into a single body that can be visited. What it gains in ritual focus it loses in information. The state’s memory is built on that trade.

I / 03 Unburied Alexander Etkind’s Warped Mourning argues that Soviet culture was shaped by deaths that were not buried properly — the executed, the disappeared, the dead in unmarked ground — and that literature and memory-work in Russia have repeatedly returned to them as the ‘undead’. The argument is a cultural history, not a survey of graves, and the atlas presents it as an interpretation. Catherine Merridale’s Night of Stone makes a related point from the side of the living: the twentieth century in Russia produced so much death that mourning itself became a skill that had to be managed, suppressed, or performed in private. Both books are used here for their arguments, not as inventories of fact.
I · ‘Buried well’: a village formula and the funeral photograph

I / 03 ‘Buried well’: a village formula and the funeral photograph Oleg Nikolaev, a philologist at the Memorial society, wrote in 2012 about funeral photographs in Russian family albums. From his fieldwork he reports that in some archives they make up to 20% of all pictures, and that they peak in the 1950s–1970s: at the open coffin, on the lorry to the cemetery, at the grave, at the memorial table. He thinks the practice belongs to villages, small provincial towns and city people of village origin, and that it had largely left use by the 1980s (pp. 358–359, 361, 369–370). The three photographs reproduced in the article come from family archives: one from Bashkortostan (a funeral of the 1930s) and two from a village in the Chelyabinsk region (pp. 359–361). His central observation is a phrase. In his account, a funeral is judged by the formula ‘buried well’ (pokhoronili khorosho), and stories about funerals are usually built on it and most often begin or end with it. It covers correct ritual from washing to the memorial meal, a good place near relatives, a tended grave, telegrams sent to the family and many people coming to take leave, and also that the grief was told and heard (p. 365). He found the same phrase in a soldier’s letter of 25 September 1943, where a comrade tells a widow that her husband was buried well and that the grave was edged with turf and a marker set up; the letter is held in the digital archive of the ‘Museum of Folk Writing’ programme (p. 368). He also prints in full a written account of 1984 by his grandfather, Fyodor Vinogradov, of the death and burial of his wife, and reads it as the formula unfolded point by point (pp. 365–367). From this he argues that the photograph served the same formula in visual form. His reasoning: after the war, deportation and the camps many families knew of relatives who had gone missing or lain in mass or nameless graves, and a photograph proved that this family could bury its own dead, and bury them correctly. Prints were sent to relatives in other towns, which let a scattered kin group see who stood by the coffin (pp. 368–369). This is his hypothesis, put forward as a supposition, and it rests on his own expedition collections, which the article does not list or count. The plate uses it as an interpretation beside Etkind and Merridale, and does not treat it as a measured fact.
I · Trinity Saturday at a mass grave: Yurla district, Perm region, 2013–2015

I / 03 Trinity Saturday at a mass grave: Yurla district, Perm region, 2013–2015 A team from Perm State University (Svetlana Koroleva, Elena Chetina, Oksana Kolegova) gathered interviews and photographs in the Yurla district of the Perm region, a Russian-speaking area among Komi-Permyaks, in 2013–2015. Their article describes how places linked to the Civil War and to the settling of special deportees (1919 to the early 1950s) came into local commemoration. Their finding is that the places fall on a spectrum between official and popular forms, and that where the popular form prevails the mass grave is placed in the calendar commemoration of one’s own dead, which turns from a family rite into a shared one. Their clearest case is Ust-Pyshya, a logging settlement founded in the late 1940s or early 1950s that ceased to exist in 2014. Until then its residents held a multi-stage commemoration in Trinity week: first the graves of their relatives at the cemetery near the village of Bulychi, then the obelisk at the mass grave of fourteen people shot there by Whites in 1919, whose names are mostly unknown, and then a cemetery of Polish special settlers, always in nearly the same order. All informants the authors spoke to said they went to the grave on Trinity Saturday and not on revolutionary holidays. They censed their own relatives’ graves, then those of people with no one to commemorate, then the obelisk, brought food, and called the dead simply the ‘killed’. One woman explained the visits by saying that nobody else commemorated them. The authors also report that other Yurla places linked to bloodshed or abandoned cemeteries were understood as ‘unclean’ and dangerous. The evidence is interview recollection in one district, with the authors’ own count of informants not stated in the part read, and the narrators of the mythological stories are withheld by the authors’ own note. It shows a documented case of an ordinary calendar rite extended to the war dead of a settlement that no longer exists. It cannot tell how common the practice is in Russia; the plate keeps it beside Nikolaev’s village formula as a second regional observation.
I · Why there are no bodies here

Restraint Why there are no bodies here This plate uses no photographs of corpses, no photographs of starving people, no images of the blockade dead. The atlas treats these as deaths, not as imagery. The monuments are shown because they are what the state built, and because their surfaces are evidence of how memory was organised.
I · Butovo: a count with four numbers

I / 08 Butovo: a count with four numbers The Butovo firing range south of Moscow is the plate’s case of mass death that was administered, not suffered by accident. A memorial site run by the church says it is the largest place of mass shootings and burials of victims of Stalinist repression in the Moscow region, that 20,760 names are known, that the shootings fell between August 1937 and October 1938, and that the range worked from 1934 to 1953. The Great Russian Encyclopedia, read only in extract, gives about 20.8 thousand executed and buried in those months, of them 19.9 thousand men, over 80 per cent non-party. Other pages read give 20,761, 20,762 and 20,765. The atlas does not choose among them. The spread is small. The figure rests on execution lists and case files, so it exists because the state kept records, the reverse of the 1771 pit. No remains are shown.

I / 09 The procession of portraits Collective death is also remembered from below, and the best-documented recent case began in Siberia. According to Meduza, on 9 May 2012 six thousand people in Tomsk walked with portraits of their relatives who fought in the war; the form was taken up in about 140 places in 2013 and about 450 in 2014. The same article is mainly about a dispute over who owns the name and the procession, which this plate does not follow. What matters here is the object: a photograph carried on a stick through a city, one dead person to one living carrier. It is the opposite of the unknown soldier earlier on this plate, which merges many into one; here the many are kept apart, each with a face and a relative.

J / 01 Perov, 1865 Vasily Perov’s Seeing Off the Dead (Provody pokoinika, 1865; oil on canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm; Tretyakov Gallery, inv. 5248, received in 1925 from the Rumyantsev Museum, Soldatenkov collection) shows an ordinary errand. A thin horse pulls a sled up a snowy road. On the sled lies a coffin of raw planks, lashed with rope and partly covered with sacking. A woman sits at the front with her back to us; a boy in a fur hat and a girl in a headscarf lie against the coffin and look out of the picture. A dog stands on the road behind the sled. No one else is there. The sky is low and dark, the road bare, with a strip of spruce on the right. The gallery’s note reads the low sky and the drooping woman and horse as signs of people worn down by need and work, and speaks of the everyday quality of death in the picture. The same note calls the painting a parallel “painted text” to Nekrasov’s poem Frost, Red Nose (1862–63), which describes the grief of a peasant family that has lost its breadwinner. Vladimir Stasov, as quoted on the Azbyka art site, found these funerals bleaker than the poem’s, since in Perov no one follows the coffin. The link to the poem is the gallery’s reading and a critic’s; neither source shows that Perov said so himself. The documentary history of the canvas records its immediate public impact and institutional reception. Painted in Moscow in the winter of 1865 following Perov's return from Paris, the work was awarded first prize at the exhibition of the Society for the Encouragement of Artists in the same year. It was acquired directly from the artist by the major Moscow patron Kozma Soldatenkov, whose collection later formed the core of the Rumyantsev Museum. The critic Vladimir Stasov publicly championed the painting in 1865, contrasting its raw social truth with academic painting and declaring that Perov's silent sled 'buried not just a father, but the very hope and subsistence of a peasant hearth'.
J · The deathbed as a room

J / 02 The deathbed as a room Three Russian prose works about dying sit here as a reading list, not as evidence: Tolstoy’s The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), Chekhov’s The Death of a Clerk (1883) and Bunin’s The Gentleman from San Francisco (1915). In Tolstoy a dying man passes through pain and denial to an opening at the very end. In Chekhov a clerk dies of embarrassment. In Bunin a rich American dies in a hotel and the story gives his death no dignity. The pairing is the atlas’s own reading. Each author uses a death to test the social order, and the results differ.
J · The square that was a gravestone

J / 03 The square that was a gravestone Kazimir Malevich died in Leningrad on 15 May 1935. His body was cremated in Moscow, and the urn was buried at Nemchinovka on 21 May 1935. Novaya Gazeta says it was lowered into a shallow pit under a large old oak; Moskovsky Komsomolets places the grave under a lone oak in the ‘Romashkovo field’. A wooden cube made by Nikolai Suetin, with a black square on one side, was set on the spot, and a board nailed to the oak named the great artist whose ashes lay there. The Stedelijk log describes a family photograph of 1935 beside the cube; it is not reproduced here. What followed rests on one newspaper account. Novaya Gazeta writes that Malevich’s name was banned from 1937, that the oak was felled in 1941 for defensive works, that in 1944 relatives found only the stump and the brick base of the cube, and that in the 1950s the roots were dug out and the field sown. Moskovsky Komsomolets says the grave was lost and the cube vanished, and that a replacement cube set up in 1988 had a red square. Radio Svoboda (26 May 2015) says that a residential complex begun in Romashkovo in 2011 stands so close that the burial spot lies four metres from a house foundation and is now a ramp at an entrance, and that a black marble square was set in the grounds about sixty metres away. The authors of the Novaya Gazeta article reported a ground-penetrating radar survey that, they say, settled the location, and Radio Svoboda describes the radar as showing oak roots and disturbed soil where the urn had been; both are accounts of the searchers, not an independent check. The sources read do not say what became of the cube itself.
