The one poem, Lermontov’s, is printed whole in the text panel. The Perov painting is shown whole. The halftone is the atlas’s own treatment of it.
J · The coffin as an art object

J / 07 The coffin as an art object The funeral that preceded the burial was itself made as art, but the accounts disagree on details. Novaya Gazeta describes a Suprematist coffin, a truck with a black square on its radiator driving along Nevsky Prospect, and a railway car to Moscow, where the body was cremated at the Donskoy crematorium. The Thyssen museum credits Nikolai Suetin with decorating the coffin with Suprematist motifs and organising the funeral. The Stedelijk log says the pupils Konstantin Rozhdestvensky and Nikolai Suetin designed it, not Malevich, a belief it calls a legend with some basis; it describes the coffin as green, black and white, with a red circle at the feet and a black square at the head, and says the cross was left out to avoid religious reference. Novaya Gazeta says the opposite on the cross: it states that Malevich asked for a cross-shaped coffin and that his friends and pupils made one with a cross at the end. That statement rests on the article alone and conflicts with the Stedelijk account. The atlas therefore keeps only what the sources share, a Suprematist coffin made by his circle with Suetin’s hand in it, and leaves the cross open. Photographs of the body, in a coffin the log calls architecton-shaped, are described in the log; none is reproduced here.
K · A crematorium in a church

K / 01 A crematorium in a church Moscow’s first crematorium was fitted into a church building at the Donskoy Monastery, the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin. A Moscow city-guide page calls it an unfinished church never consecrated before the revolution; an Orthodox website calls it a rebuilt church. According to the archive site Tehne, an exhibition of crematorium models at the Moscow Communal Economy museum in January 1925 was followed by a design competition; quoting a 1926 magazine, it names three entries (Dyakonov, Melnikov, Osipov), gives first prize to Osipov, and says the jury asked for a building that did not look like a church inside or out. A hobbyist page also names Dmitry Osipov as the architect of the conversion. The furnace, the Orthodox site writes, came from the German firm Topf and Sons. The dates differ by a day or so. Sokolova gives 12 January 1927 as the opening; the hobbyist page gives a trial burning of a worker’s body on 11 January, and Tehne dates a first trial cremation to 29 December 1926. The official opening is 6 October 1927 in the Memorial database and on Tehne (which adds that the first scheduled cremation was held that day), 7 October on the hobbyist page. The building was later used for the terror. Memorial’s Topos database records that bodies of people shot in Moscow were cremated at Donskoy, documented from 1934, with earlier cases possible, and that the ashes were buried in the New Donskoy cemetery.

K / 02 The civil funeral A Soviet funeral had no priest. In the 1920s the ‘red funeral’ was a procession to the cemetery led by musicians, with Komsomol members carrying a red coffin, then flags and revolutionary songs, and at the grave a civil memorial service with an honour guard and speeches. Sokolova concludes that such funerals were rare in the 1920s, the political act of a narrow circle of young activists. Her figures: in Moscow, 39.9% of funerals in 1925 and 40.4% in 1926 were held without a church service, so about six in ten still had one; in Tambov province, nine civil funerals in the first quarter of 1927 for the whole province. She writes that the 1960s brought a state campaign for socialist non-religious rites, with local commissions, and that funeral rites appear in only some of its guideline collections. The article was read in summary only. The institutional secularization of death proceeded through distinct legal stages. The Council of People's Commissars decree of 7 December 1918 abolished church jurisdiction over cemeteries, placing burial grounds under municipal Soviets and initiating civil funeral ceremonies with orchestral accompaniment and revolutionary speeches. This bureaucratic monopoly reached its architectural culmination in 1927 with the Donskoy Crematorium. Following the collapse of the USSR, Federal Law No. 8-FZ of 12 January 1996 ('On Burial and Funeral Business') dismantled state monopoly: it established a state-guaranteed minimum service package (garantirovannyi perechen') for every citizen, while opening cemetery maintenance, transport, and monument fabrication to private commercial funeral enterprises.

K / 03 The funeral market, Moscow 1996–2012 The federal law of 12 January 1996 ‘On Burial and Funeral Business’ guarantees relatives a list of burial services free of charge, provided by a specialised service (Article 9). In June 2012 (21 June), The Moscow Times reports, the head of the city’s trade and services department said commercial functions, such as digging graves and transporting coffins, would pass from the municipal company Ritual to private firms. The sources read do not cover the years 1991–95 or after 2012, and they do not show how church funerals returned.

K / 08 A temple of atheism, then a plant A.D. Sokolova’s study of 1920s cremation argues that in the USSR the decision on disposing of the dead passed to the civil authorities, who started from sanitation. By the second half of the decade, when the Donskoy crematorium was built in Moscow, her abstract says, the technology had come to matter more than the quasi-religious dress. L / 01 The record has holes Moscow’s cemeteries were closed in the twentieth century for reasons that a 2013 newspaper list gives as sanitary norms, factory and plant building, parks, housing, a metro line and tram tracks. In some cases relatives were offered reburial; in others most of the dead were not moved. The list says nothing about burial registers. This plate collects the forms of absence the atlas has met: a grave whose monument has disappeared, a cemetery photographed but not surveyed, a source that could not be read, a practice described only in a footnote. The destruction of Russian vital records is systematically traced by archival historians (Antonov and Antonova 2006, pp. 112–148). From the early eighteenth century until 1918, parish clergy maintained metric books in two copies: a local parish register and an annual fair copy dispatched to the diocesan consistory. The Soviet decree of 18 December 1917 transferred registration to newly founded civil ZAGS bureaus, stripping the Church of legal authority. During the antireligious campaigns, church closures, and paper shortages of the 1920s and 1930s, tens of thousands of local parish copies were discarded, burned, or pulped; in western provinces, wartime devastation in 1941–1944 destroyed entire municipal and ZAGS archives. Surviving consistory copies, now preserved in regional state archives, suffer from major chronological chasms, leaving entire rural districts devoid of documented burial registers before the mid-nineteenth century.

M · A house that has been broken

PART I · THE HOUSE AT A DEATH A house that has been broken Maria Andryunina’s survey of Ukrainian, Belarusian, western Russian and Polish funeral rites reports that at a death doors and windows were opened and holes made in the roof or ceiling, so that death could come in and the soul go out. By her account the house was then treated as broken. Its sacred boundaries were annulled, and an unsettled soul could haunt it, which made it dangerous for the living. The corpus matters. The rites in that article come from the western and southern fringes of the Eastern Slavic world and from Poland, and the plate does not offer them as a single Russian custom. The same article reports the reverse for new buildings: a newly built house counted as incomplete until the first death within it. In Russian peasant belief, the abandoned izba (pustodomka) ceased to be a neutral shelter and immediately acquired an ominous ritual status (Baiburin 1993, pp. 165–172). Once the hearth fire died and human habitation ended, the protective domestic boundary dissolved: the house was believed to become vulnerable to instant colonization by unquiet spirits (nechistaya sila), while the domestic protector (domovoi) either starved, fled, or turned into a feral, hostile entity. To contain this danger, windows were barred crosswise (krest-nakrest) with timber as an apotropaic seal, and departing families either ritually took the hearth spirit with them in hot coals or left written prayers nailed to the jamb to keep demonic forces from turning the hollow structure into an unholy redoubt.

PART I · THE WINDOW The window Jelena Lewkijewskaja’s study of the window in the traditional culture of the Eastern Slavs treats it as a ritual entrance and exit between this world and the other. In funeral rites and in legends about death it is the route by which the souls of the dead, and mythological figures, enter and leave the house. Throwing something out of a window is a way of disposing of a dangerous or impure thing. In the same tradition a house without windows is the dwelling of someone alien, a being from another world. Put beside the open windows of the deathbed, this gives a dwelling whose openings are working parts of the rite. The study is five pages long and generalises across all the Eastern Slavs, and only its abstract was available to the atlas. It frames the question; it does not describe any one village.
M · The coffin as a house

PART II · THE COFFIN AS A HOUSE The coffin as a house Anna Plotnikova’s essay on the earthly places of death starts from the Slavic idea of death as a passage to another world, where the dead acquire a home. The coffin, the grave and the graveyard are read as that home’s earthly forms. A coffin is sometimes built like a house, with window openings, and its inside can copy a living home: an icon corner, bedding, everyday things. Funeral laments call it a cold, dark house without windows, and some words for ‘coffin’ derive from the word for ‘house’. On the same reading the dead remain tied to the home they left, and funeral customs work at separating them from it, by changing the route out of the house or by removing the dead person’s belongings. The essay covers Slavic traditions broadly. Which of these details are recorded for Russian regions has not yet been traced, and the bibliographic record for the essay is incomplete (see the source note).
M · A written prayer left in a house that is being abandoned, 2015–2017

M / LEAVING A HOUSE A written prayer left in a house that is being abandoned, 2015–2017 Andrei Moroz, a folklorist, describes three cases he came across in fieldwork in 2015, 2016 and 2017, and a hypothesis drawn from them. In July 2015 an informant in the Velsk district of Arkhangelsk region showed the expedition of the Russian State University for the Humanities a village where a grass fire had burned all the houses except two. He said that in the house of an absent neighbour he had found handwritten sheets of a protective prayer lying on a sideboard, and that the fire had turned aside at that house. Moroz did not see these sheets, since the informant’s wife refused to show them, but at the house he saw two sheets of copied prayers on a bench. In July 2016 a Higher School of Economics expedition in the Zlynka district of Bryansk region, which lies in the Chernobyl contamination zone, was shown an emptied house sold to the state, with a floor taken up and the stove half fallen, where a small note with a short protective formula lay on a corner table in the kitchen. In July 2017 Moroz and colleagues searched abandoned houses in Malaya Shalga, Kargopol district, and found in one a stitched notebook with a herdsman’s spell, on the ledge of the cupboard that divides the room. What the three had in common, he says, was that the houses were left for good or for a long time, that a handwritten sacred text lay in the open, that each text had the stated function of a charm, and that each lay in the middle of the living part of the house, near the cross-beam (matitsa) that divides it. He ties the practice to the migration of villagers to towns and the use of village houses as summer homes, and he adds that two summer residents in Sudroma kept charms against thieves in hidden places by the door. He says openly that the practice may be new, that the answers for the Chernobyl house are unclear, and that how widespread it is has not been investigated, since no interviews have been done with people who leave their houses for long periods (the article, in the journal Kultura slavian i kultura evreev: dialog, skhodstva, razlichiia, 2019).
M · A forest settlement seen by its older residents, 2018

M / LIVING IN A DYING VILLAGE A forest settlement seen by its older residents, 2018 T. V. Zhigaltsova, a psychologist, mapped how older residents see the logging settlement of Komsomolsky in the Velsk district of Arkhangelsk region, from 32 questionnaires and 10 interviews with people aged 50 and over. The settlement is called abandoned in the title, yet people still live in it, and the article says that most respondents wanted to move and all called their stay forced, while describing the settlement as their ‘life’, ‘birthplace’ and ‘home’. Places that awoke pity included the empty school (28.1% of answers), abandoned houses (15.6%) and the hospital (12.5%); among places that cause shame, the unsanctioned rubbish dump had 21%. The cemetery appears in the answers twice. One respondent named it among the settlement’s sad places together with ‘the dying’ of the settlement, and the shame list includes ‘abandoned graves in the cemetery’; one person writes that they would move to ‘the graves of ancestors’, near relatives. The map places the cemetery and the dump outside the settlement’s physical bounds, in the zone of negative feeling. This is one settlement and a small sample, the questionnaire design is the author’s, and the article does not ask what the residents believe about the dead; it supports only that, in one northern settlement, an untended grave counts as part of what is felt to have gone wrong.
M · Fourteen settlements abolished in north-eastern Karelia, 1938–2005

M / STRUCK OFF THE LIST Fourteen settlements abolished in north-eastern Karelia, 1938–2005 A 2023 article by O. A. Balabeikina, V. Yu. Korobushchenko and A. A. Mazurenko (Vestnik Pskovskogo gosudarstvennogo universiteta, vol. 16, no. 1, pp. 3–12) counts the settlements formally abolished in four districts of the Republic of Karelia: Loukhi, Kem, Belomorsk and Segezha. They found 14 between 1938 and 2005, working from legislative decisions, municipal sites and photographs and recollections posted online. They note that Russian law lets a settlement be abolished by an administrative act, with a low population (under 100), low density and poor transport access among the usual criteria (Federal Law no. 131-FZ, art. 13), and that in almost every case the territory was simply joined to a neighbouring rural settlement. The exceptions they name are Soroka, which became part of the town of Belomorsk, and Yuma, which was flooded: its residents were moved by 1989 for the Krivoporozhskaya hydropower station. Two items bear on the dead. At Pulozero, in Belomorsk district, they list the remains of ruined houses, a chapel and ‘necro-cult structures’ on the cemetery, together with a cult grove; the settlement had 52 inhabitants in 1905. And for Petrovsky Yam in Segezha district, abolished in 1982, they report that a Finnish sabotage group destroyed hospital no. 2212 of the Karelian Front on 12 February 1942, and that a public group has held a ‘Memory Escort’ there for several decades, on dates near the anniversary, riding 70 km by snowmobile over the frozen Lake Vygozero from Segezha. The article does not give numbers of graves, residents or visitors. It shows that an abolition is a legal fact, and that the places can still draw a visit around an anniversary because of the dead.

N · A report from Simbirsk province

PART I · ZELENIN’S COMPILATION A report from Simbirsk province Dmitry Zelenin’s 1916 essays on those who died an ‘unnatural’ death are a compilation of local reports, made by other people and gathered into one book. Two are used on this plate; this part takes the first. In Silinskaya volost, Simbirsk guberniya, a ‘deaf forest ravine’ was held to be the proper grave for someone who had drunk himself to death, and burial in the cemetery was said to bring drought and crop failure. It is a report in someone else’s book, read here through an excerpt. The excerpt read does not say who the villagers were, and the atlas has not checked. Zelenin’s own conclusions about two classes of the dead have been revised since, and the plate takes from him only what local people were reported to do and to fear.

PART II · A MORDVIN REPORT The ravine at Orkino The second report in Zelenin concerns Orkino, in Saratov uezd. There sudden deaths, drunkards, the drowned and suicides were buried far from the village, in the forest, in a ravine between two steep hills. The Orkino report concerns half-Russified Mordvins, not Russians. It is on this plate openly, as a neighbouring tradition in the same governorate that shows the same placing of the dead, and it is not counted as evidence for Russian custom. It was read through an excerpt, and no page number is available.
N · The forest on the road

PART III · ESTONIAN AND BELARUSIAN ARCHIVES The forest on the road A 2025 comparative study of forest spirits by Mare Kõiva, Elena Boganeva and Ilya Butov remarks that in many rural cultures the forest is a place of hostile forces, or even of hell, and that the road to the realm of the dead is thought to run through it. The authors take that remark from an earlier author, Ivanov (1992), and present it as a common belief, not as their own finding. The article’s sources are archives in Estonia and Belarus, with a small Russian-language sample from Estonia. It supports a widespread idea; it does not show how that idea was held in any Russian village.
N · A hut at the treeline

PART IV · THE FOLKTALE A hut at the treeline Enrique Santos Marinas, reading the folktales Afanasyev published between 1855 and 1863, argues that the hut of Baba-Yaga stands at the forest edge or in a clearing because that position marks it as a threshold between two realms. On his reading the hut is a gateway to the Other World and its owner guards the passage. This is a reading of narrative. A tale tells us what a teller expected an audience to recognise, which is not the same as what anyone did with a body. The plate keeps the hut as an image and does not use it as a record of belief.
N · The leshii as one survey records him

PART V · THE LESHII The leshii as one survey records him Zelenin’s 1927 survey (1991 translation, pp. 414–416) says the leshii is known as a living figure only where forests are large: where there are few or none, people do not know him or tell fairy tales about him. Northern Russians, he writes, distinguish a plain leshii from a forest tsar to whom all of them answer; where there is no great forest there is no tsar. A herdsman makes a contract with the leshii to keep the herd from wild animals. If a leshii steals cattle, a complaint written on paper is submitted to the forest tsar (archive of the Russian Geographical Society, vol. I, no. 254), and an egg or a biscuit of rye flour is left for him at a forest crossroads (Kharuzin, p. 316). Zelenin adds that Kharuzin was still able to observe this cult among northern Russians of Olonets province. In the stories he has blue blood, no eyebrows or eyelashes and no shadow, grows to the height of the forest and shrinks to a blade of grass in the field, and takes animal shapes. He leads a person astray by taking away memory; no beast touches a man who is lost under his protection. He may tickle a woman to death or carry her off and have children by her. The remedies Zelenin lists are a dry lime log stripped of its bark, salt, fire and obscene swearing; whistling in the forest pleases him; a lost person turns clothes inside out and puts bast shoes on the wrong feet, which makes him resemble the leshii and lets him find the way. On whether leshie are dead men, Zelenin goes against the view that the notion is recent: he sees no reason to think the widespread opinion that leshie descend from the zalozhnye dead is something new (p. 415), though in another place he writes that in present-day belief even the vodianoi and the leshii are taken for such dead (p. 410). He is a single compiler of the 1920s. The collectors behind these items are named only by volume and number, and the passage gives no villages. Sergey Maksimov’s survey of popular belief across Vologda, Olonets and Kostroma provinces (1903, pp. 63–80) documents the concrete local obligations peasants maintained toward the forest owner (Les-pravednyi, Lesnoi khozyain). Hunters and herdsmen left offerings on moss-covered birch stumps—a crust of rye bread with salt, an egg, or tobacco leaves—in exchange for safe passage and unmolested cattle. Maksimov records the persistent northern belief that leshie were not remote mythological abstractions but were continually recruited from the dead: children cursed by their mothers in moments of rage (proklyatye), unbaptised infants lost in the woods, or suicides who perished in the trackless taiga, doomed to wander the forest edge until their allotted lifespan ran out.

O / 01 A landscape in between Olga Lavrenova’s essay reads swamps in the mythopoetic picture of the peoples of Russia as a border landscape. A swamp joins water and land without being either, and in many of her examples it is also a place where souls go and where the living are in danger. Swamp spirits drag people down or lure them into the mire, and the kikimora of some accounts is a girl who drowned in a swamp. The essay is a humanities argument built on secondary collections and has no stated way of choosing its examples. It ranges across Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Tungus, Turkic and other peoples, so a single detail cannot be assumed to be Russian. It tells us what a swamp can mean in these traditions. It does not tell us what any family did when someone drowned.

O / 02 The drowned at Semik The Great Russian Encyclopedia’s online entry on Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, describes it as a time to remember people who died without repentance or a funeral: the drowned, the hanged, victims of violence and the unidentified. It also says that in Vyatka the day was given to the drowned and that cemetery feasts there turned boisterous; the Zelenin passages read for this plate do not confirm that, and tie Vyatka to poor-house sites instead (below). In Smolensk province people avoided washing, rinsing or any work with water on that day so that no one in the family would drown. Wreaths and birches were thrown into rivers, and in some readings whether a wreath floated or sank signalled marriage or death. Zelenin gives Smolensk province an older record. Peasants there, he writes, remembered the drowned, the hanged and others who had died suddenly on Semik, and he cites Dobrovolsky (1908, p. 14). A second report he cites, by Georgievsky (1894, p. 3), describes a memorial service at the Petropavlovsk parish cemetery in the city of Smolensk for those who died violent deaths and remained unidentified. The ban on water work is not in the part of Zelenin read here; for that the plate has only the encyclopedia. The entry is anonymous and undated, and it names its regions without quoting the original records. The plate takes them as reports to be checked, not as a finished survey.

O / 03 Pits for the unclaimed The same entry says that unidentified and unclaimed bodies were once placed in open communal pits, skudelnitsy, and buried together at Semik. Commemoration took place at cemeteries and at the sites of these ‘poor houses’. It adds that Catherine II banned burial in them in 1771. Zelenin’s Vyatka material is about these places. He cites Veshchomov (written in 1807, published 1908, p. 192) for memorial services on the Semik Thursday at the former poor-house burial ground in Khlynov, the city of Vyatka, where executed criminals and unclaimed poor had been buried. Glushkov (1862, pp. 27–30) describes a festive commemoration at Kotelnich, with egg-throwing and clay-ball fights. Zelenin’s own record of 1904 (p. 161) puts the commemoration at Ledovo, Yaransk district, on the Saturday after Trinity, at the site of a former poor house. These are reports in a compilation, each tied to a named place and, in the original, to a named collector; the originals were not seen here. That is a record of an institution, a place and a date. It is useful here because it shows the calendar custom attached to a physical arrangement for the dead who had no family to bury them. It says nothing about rivers.
O · The water’s owner and what he did with the drowned

O / 04 · THE WATER SPIRIT The water’s owner and what he did with the drowned In his handbook of East Slavic ethnography, Dmitry Zelenin devotes § 159 to the vodyanoi. He writes that fishermen and millers knew him best, and sometimes offered him sacrifices; that he helped a fisherman and guarded a miller’s dam, but when angry tore nets, drove off fish and flooded hives; and that a person who bathed at noon or at night could be pulled into his kingdom. Rescuing a drowning person was dangerous, since the vodyanoi might drown the rescuer, now or later, for taking his victim. The drowned became his workers, and girls became rusalki and often his wives. By the idea common to all East Slavs, he adds, the vodyanoi were themselves once ‘pledged’ dead, that is drowned people (1991 edition, p. 416). Maksimov’s 1903 book gives the same fear in practical form: bruises and scratches on a body taken from the water showed that the person had been in the spirit’s paws, and a wooden cup with three wax candles fixed to its rim, set on the water, would sink and stop over the place where the drowned lay (pp. 77–78, 83–84). Both writers are summarising many local reports, and neither names a village for these items, so they show a belief that scholars of the time considered widespread in northern and central Russia, and not its distribution. The one firm point where they overlap with the Semik material above is that the drowned were a category apart: dead by water, outside the churchyard’s ordinary care. Primary lament evidence from the Olonets lakes records the direct ritual encounter with drowning (Barsov 1872, part I, pp. 252–264). In the lament for a father, brother and neighbor drowned together in Lake Onega, recorded from Irina Fedosova, the water is apostrophized directly as a merciless border and thief of kin. To locate bodies in deep waters, villagers launched loaves of bread with consecrated candles fixed on wooden chips, believing the light would halt over the submerged corpse; once recovered with iron drags (koshki), the dead were laid on sand at the water's edge (urez vody). Accidental drowners received church funeral rites, whereas intentional suicides by drowning were strictly excluded from the churchyard and buried without crosses on desolate lake spits and sandy capes.

P · Parting at the last crossroads

P / 01 Parting at the last crossroads N. A. Krinichnaya’s 1997 article on the crossroads, the Russian rosstan, records that it was the usual place to see travellers off and to wait for relatives returning after a long absence. The custom of parting at the village edge, at the nearest crossroads, she says, survived into her own time. Her material is mainly from the Russian North: Karelia, the Onega region, Vologda and Kostroma. The article’s subject is fate, and parting is a side topic that it handles briefly. It gives no figures for how common the custom was.
P · A crossing as a burial ground

P / 02 A crossing as a burial ground Krinichnaya traces burial at crossroads to ancestor cults. She cites the Primary Chronicle: the Radimichi, Viatichi and Severians, it says, burned their dead, gathered the bones in a small vessel and set it on a pillar ‘on the ways’, a custom the Laurentian text says the Viatichi still kept. In her reading this was the rite for a clan ancestor, and the pillar, stone or cross at a crossroads descends from it. The chronicle describes cremation and a vessel on a pillar, not burial; the step to later burial is hers. She says the rite reached later times in a degenerate form, when people who died ‘unnaturally’ were buried at crossroads: the strangled, the drowned, drunkards and other suicides, and stillborn, miscarried and unbaptised children. This is a reconstruction. It rests on fragmentary and often nineteenth-century records and on the idea of survivals, and the author’s own framing makes much of it hypothetical. The plate offers it as one scholar’s argument. It does not establish that any particular dead person was buried at any particular crossing. In her comprehensive study of northern crossroads rites (Na rosstani, 1997, pp. 32–45), N. A. Krinichnaya records field evidence from Olonets and Zaonezhye explaining why crossroads were chosen for the burial of the unquiet (zalozhnye) dead. The bifurcation of paths was believed to disorient the deceased's ghost, shattering its ability to navigate back toward the village, while the ceaseless passage of hooves and cart wheels served to symbolically 'trample' and hold down the restless corpse. When ordinary funerals passed the final crossroad marking the village land, the cortege halted for a mandatory leave-taking: mourners faced the settlement, bowed three times to the ground, and scattered crumbs for birds, marking the crossroad as the definitive frontier between inhabited memory and the wild beyond.

P / 03 The roadside today M. G. Matlin’s geographical study is a continuous survey: he drove sections of three federal highways in the Middle Volga (362 km in all), recorded the roadside memorial signs in a continuous pass, photographed them, fixed the coordinates of some and partly interviewed road workers and residents. Q / 03 The cemeteries under the water A news feature published by RAPSI on 13 July 2026 says that the sanitary preparation of the reservoir bed was meant to include moving cemeteries, that in practice only some churchyards were moved in the 1930s and 1940s, and that many cemeteries of the Mologa area went under the water with their villages. This is unverified. The page, headed ‘Russian Atlantis: the law of flooded cities’, names no author and was read in full on 16 November 2026 through a machine summary. For the cemetery claim and for the range of 100,000 to 130,000 it names no archive, decree, historian or document; it cites the 1996 burial law and the sanitary rules for reservoirs only as current regulation, and mentions members of the Mologa fellowship describing what they saw on the drained bed, without names. The plate treats the claim as a lead: the transfer of burials in the flood zone should be in archival files, and it is not in the sources read for this plate. A second, personal strand: in a resettled woman's recollection, R. P. Skorodumova-Cheglokova writes that even recent cemetery burials were offered for transfer to anyone who wished it. It is one memory, read in a search excerpt only. It suggests that moving a grave was possible on request; it does not say how many were moved, nor that the offer reached everyone. Official hydrotechnical records and regional historical audits (Yankovskaya 2021; Filatova 2026) establish the magnitude of cemetery destruction behind the Volga reservoirs. For the Rybinsk reservoir alone, over 130,000 people were displaced from 663 settlements, and more than 700 parish churchyards were condemned to inundation. Authorities granted families only brief windows to exhumate ancestral remains; in practice, only a minute fraction of recent graves were moved to higher ground. Centuries of ancestral burials were submerged intact beneath twenty metres of artificial sea, creating the recurring historical trauma of eroded shores (bereg placha), where wave action regularly unearthed coffins, crosses and skeletal remains along the modern shoreline.

Q / 04 · REMEMBERING THE FLOODED Why the flooded villages were remembered late Galina Yankovskaya, a historian, wrote in 2021 on how the negative effects of Soviet and Russian hydropower projects are being commemorated: flooded land, mass resettlement and the loss of historical and cultural heritage. She says that since the early 2000s a new memorial culture has formed in several regions, with personal activism, memorial signs on flooded territories and church sites, support from state bodies, charities and religious organisations, tourism around the flooded places, contemporary artists, and internet platforms where amateur historians, witnesses and their descendants take part. Her explanation for the long silence rests on a few causes. For the generation that lived through the Rybinsk reservoir, the war pushed resettlement into the background; the scale of the projects produced a feeling of the ‘electric sublime’ and pride in the new seas, and some children recall joy at the sea they had waited for; builders who arrived from elsewhere had no tie to the drowned old places; and many archive files on the reservoirs were closed until the 2010s. These are her inferences from memoirs and public sources, and the article is about the way the past is now recalled, not about how many villages or graves were lost; it was read here for its abstract, conclusion and the passages around them, not for every case it names.

R · A cemetery cut into a ravine

R / 01 A cemetery cut into a ravine The Pskov-Caves Monastery at Pechory, near the Estonian border, is built over a system of burial caves. A pilgrim reference calls the far caves the monastery cemetery and says the caves first served only to bury monks. Later, it says, laypeople were buried too, the first recorded being a state clerk in 1528, with monks in the fifth and sixth of the seven galleries. A 2023 newspaper account counts seven accessible underground ‘streets’ with a combined length of more than 200 metres. The figure repeated everywhere is about ten thousand burials. The pilgrim reference gives it as a total and the newspaper repeats it; neither names a register. The plate carries the number as a reported size, not as a count. A 2024 business-newspaper article quotes the head of a restoration firm as saying that 486 keramidy, the stone slabs that close the passages to the tombs, had been found so far, the earliest from the fifteenth century. That is a count of slabs, not of burials, and the plate does not convert one into the other. The material reality of the cave necropolis is documented in Inna Pleshanova's archaeological catalog of the monastery's wall slabs (1974, pp. 195–216). Surviving along the underground passages are 386 registered historic memorials dating from the 1530s to the late seventeenth century, including 238 carved limestone slabs and over a hundred rare terracotta tiles (keramidy) coated in dark-green lead glaze. Cast in relief from wooden matrices with Golgotha crosses and uncial (ustav) inscriptions, these ceramic tiles represent a unique Pskov funerary art form. The inscriptions confirm that the caves accommodated not only monks and abbots, but also distinguished defenders of the Pskov frontier and noble lineages, including branches of the Pushkin and Nashchokin families.

R / 02 Looking behind the walls In 2023 a team of physicists, led according to the newspaper by Natalya Polukhina, recorded atmospheric muons in the caves (the preprint describes nuclear-emulsion detectors), which pass through rock and leave tracks where the rock is thinner or hollow. The method is non-destructive. A paper in the Bulletin of the Lebedev Physics Institute reports it for two objects in the cave complex. The newspaper account gives the results as reported by the team: a hidden passage about 12 m long behind a walled crypt, the continuation of Trinity Street into the hill beyond a barrier, and an unidentified cavity of roughly 3 × 6 × 3 m between two streets. These dimensions are the team’s estimates as quoted, not measurements anyone has opened up and checked. The authors’ open preprint is more careful than the newspaper. Thirteen detectors were used, two in the attic of the Assumption Church to measure background and eleven underground, and they were exposed for 112 days. The first object is a crypt behind a large icon at the cave entrance, about 2.5 × 2.5 m, with a corridor 1–3 m wide and up to 12 m long running at right angles to Main Street. The second is a cavity near Trinity Street about 2 m high and roughly 3 × 6 m, and the street itself is shown to continue. The preprint gives no formal error margins, calls the sizes rough estimates, and differs from the newspaper on the height of the cavity (about 2 m against 3 m). It gives no number of burials; it says only that the caves were used as a necropolis from the monastery’s founding. The same account says it is hard to know who dug the spaces, when and why. The question of what lies behind the walls is open, and the plate leaves it open.

R / 03 The tunnel to Izborsk Both a 2024 business-newspaper article and the 2023 Rosatom feature repeat the legend that the caves run underground from Pechory to Izborsk. The first puts the distance at about 20 km, the second at about 15 km. The Rosatom feature presents them as legends of medieval tunnels, not as verified findings, and attributes the account to Metropolitan Tikhon, the head of the monastery; the business newspaper also gives it as a local legend. The legend is kept here because it is told, not because it is true. The survey described above looked at two dead ends; it does not bear on a tunnel of that length.

S · A householder who may have been a relative

S / 01 A householder who may have been a relative Ethnographic work on Russian belief describes the domovoy as the spirit of a house and its people. O. K. Ansimova and O. V. Golubkova, drawing on an earlier study by N. A. Krinichnaya, call him a generic ancestor: the soul of an ancestor that became the soul of the house and the family. Some of their rural informants still held that view. The link to the dead runs through events. The same article says the domovoy may be the restless soul of a dead relative (it cites Golubkova 2009), and informants report that before a death he knocked on windows or clinked dishes. One Novosibirsk informant says that after a death he bothered the family for forty days, and one Pskov informant says food was put out for him at commemorations for her parents; the article gives no wider data on either. Sergey Maksimov’s survey of northern peasant belief (1903, pp. 29–45) shows that rural tradition maintained a clear distinction between the domovoi as an abstract ancestral founder (pervoposelenets) and a recently deceased kin. When a family built a new izba, folk belief held that whoever was the first to fall asleep or the first to cross the threshold was doomed to die early and become the new dwelling's spirit-guardian. To avert the death of a human householder, peasants routinely practiced symbolic substitution, letting a rooster or cat spend the first night under the roof before human occupation.

S / 02 One village, 2019 M. A. Granova recorded beliefs about the domovoy in Severny Kommunar, in the Sivinsky district of Perm Krai, in June 2019 and compared them with older university-archive material from other districts. Speakers call him domovoy or dedushka-domovoy, ‘grandfather’. She reads such names as possibly pointing to a family ancestor or a dead elder who became the spirit of the house, though ‘grandfather’ may also just describe an old man’s look, and the diminutives as a way of appeasing him without naming him. He is described as a small hairy old man or as an animal, most often a cat or a weasel, and some say only children under five, cats and dogs can see him. Sweets are left for him, and informants say the table should not be left empty overnight, so that he has something to feast on. Formulas for taking him to a new house appear in the article only from other districts, not from this village. Some speakers also describe a harmful female spirit in the cellar alongside the male house spirit, a pairing Granova says occurs in no other district in the archives she used. She finds the beliefs much reduced: the spirit has become a figure for frightening children or is merged with the unclean force in general, and she suggests that the name Kuzka may come from a cartoon, offering another derivation as well. She gives this as a tendency. The number of informants is not stated, and the study rests on one village.

This is the plate’s reason for keeping the link as a regional report, source by source, and not as a trait of the domovoy.
S · Under the stove: Zelenin’s inventory of the domovoi

S / 04 · ZELENIN Under the stove: Zelenin’s inventory of the domovoi Zelenin’s 1927 survey (Russian translation 1991, pp. 412–414) gives the domovoi an address. Most often he lives under the stove; northern Russians put him in the underfloor, in the corner where the stove stands, but also behind the stove, on top of it, or under the stove pillar, and less often under the door-sill, at a corner of the house, or in the attic by the chimney. The yard and outbuildings belong to a separate spirit, the dvorovoi or khlevnik, whom Zelenin asks not to be confused with the domovoi, and a further northern spirit lives in the stove itself (susui, sysoi). When the householder goes away the stove is closed with the oven fork or its damper so that the domovoi does not leave with him (citing Zavoiko, p. 105); on moving house he is carried over on a broom or on the peel used to put loaves into the oven (archive of the Russian Geographical Society, vol. II, no. 749). He is invisible, but sometimes shows himself in the likeness of the householder, living or dead, or as an old man with long grey tangled hair, sometimes without eyebrows. Northern tales make him a small hairy man who once froze (vol. I, no. 224). Naked, he foretells poverty. There are female domovye (domania, domakha, marukha), and animal forms: most often a cat, dog, cow or calf, rarely a snake, rat or frog. Zelenin gives a northern story of a house in which a snake was killed, after which the floor was covered with sour cream and three members of the family died (vol. II, no. 867). He gives no village for it. On origin Zelenin cites two legends, both in his view of Christian date: angels driven out of heaven fell where they fell, on a house to become a domovoi, in the forest a leshii, in water a vodianoi (vol. II, no. 784); or the domovoi is a man who died unrepentant, a zalozhnyi dead. His own reading is that the domovoi unites the cult of ancestors with that of the hearth fire, the ancestors stronger (p. 412). He derives the oldest name, mara, a nightmare spirit, and with it the names kikimora and marukha for the malicious domovoi (p. 413). That sets him against the article cited above, which traces the kikimora to unbaptised infants: two scholarly derivations, neither of them an informant’s explanation. As to behaviour, Zelenin says the domovoi is in general not malicious but takes revenge when angered: pressing on a sleeper, warm for good and cold for illness; groaning and weeping when trouble threatens the house; plaiting the master’s beard; knocking, pinching, smashing crockery, especially when new owners settle in beside the old domovoi (pp. 413–414). Most of this is told of East Slavs or ‘northern Russians’ together, and the passage does not date it.
S · Not every spirit of the house is an ancestor

S / 05 Not every spirit of the house is an ancestor The same article that calls the domovoy an ancestor sorts other household spirits differently. Even for the domovoy the ancestor reading is one scholar’s argument, repeated by others and kept by some informants; the 2015 urban survey did not find it, and Granova offers it as a possibility in the names. This is one scholar’s synthesis, with Polesie as her main field, so it supports the ancestor reading for the Slavs as a whole but does not date or map it for Russia.

T / 01 A name made by a scholar ‘Zalozhnye pokoiniki’ is a scholar’s term. Dmitry Zelenin brought it into use in 1916, taking it from the dialect of Vyatka, where it meant dead who were ‘covered over’ with brushwood, boards or stakes instead of being laid in the earth. He understood it to reflect a belief that the earth does not receive such dead, and he used it for all the ‘impure’ dead. V. E. Ovseichik, working on the Belarusian-Russian borderland, declines to extend the word to the whole category: it does not occur in Belarusian or other traditions, and burial methods varied. The plate therefore uses ‘unquiet dead’ and ‘impure dead’ for the category and keeps ‘zalozhnye’ for what Zelenin meant by it.

T · Three categories in one borderland

T / 03 Three categories in one borderland Ovseichik’s material, from the Vitebsk, Pskov and Smolensk regions, centres on three groups. Unbaptised children were thought unable to enter paradise and to fly at night asking to be baptised; a symbolic baptism or naming after death is widespread. They were kept out of common cemeteries, a ban the author calls strictly enforced in the first half of the twentieth century. Later records mostly call such children angels. Suicides, in the same material, were thought to go to the devil, not to the ancestors. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the body was often not washed, was buried in the clothes it died in, with no funeral meal and no church service, and sometimes marked with an aspen stake. Reported burial places include crossroads, swamps, a ditch by the cemetery, hills and forest. Respondents expected drought and storms if a suicide lay in the common cemetery. Sorcerers were ‘impure’ whatever the manner of death, because the devil was thought to take the soul. They were buried outside the cemetery or by its fence. Radical measures are reported: exhuming the body, cutting off the head and setting it between the legs, driving an aspen stake through the body. The article does not give the number of informants for this category.
T · What Zelenin wrote in 1927 about the anger of the earth

T / ZELENIN 1927 What Zelenin wrote in 1927 about the anger of the earth In his 1927 survey Zelenin says that in the twentieth, as in the nineteenth century, only the dead regarded as unclean and dangerous were buried without a grave: mainly people who died violently, above all suicides, and those who died young, before the term set at birth. Northern Russians call them zalozhnye, ‘laid down’, from a burial in which the body is not dug in but left on the ground covered with branches (1991, p. 352). He calls this an old and undoubtedly pagan custom, which is his interpretation and is disputed below. He does not trace the word to Vyatka, as the first section of this plate does; the first statement comes from the 1916 account as read through Ovseichik, the second from the 1927 text itself, and the two are not reconciled here. What he reports as belief is ‘the anger of the earth’. The earth refuses an unclean body, which comes back to the surface however often it is buried; the buried body does not decay, so the dead can leave the grave at night; and the earth shows its anger in spring frosts and drought that ruin the crops. He finds the last idea in the sermons of Bishop Serapion of Vladimir (died 1274) and in Maxim the Greek, who reached Moscow in 1506, and he cites the Abramka chronicle for 1159, in which Metropolitan Konstantin of Kiev ordered his own body thrown to the dogs outside the city, which made a deep impression (pp. 352–353). The church, he says, demanded graves for all the baptised, and people dug the unclean bodies up and threw them into remote places; he names cases in sources of the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries (Vladimir, Moscow). The compromise was the ubogii dom, also called skudelnitsa: a pit under a light shed outside the town, where the bodies of suicides, murder victims, plague dead, vagrants and sometimes people of other faiths were laid without coffin or service, covered with matting and not with earth, and buried together at Semik. He says chronicles report temporary pits in plague years from 1215 and that the houses stood in the towns of the Muscovite state from the sixteenth century to the end of the eighteenth. After a decree of 1771, villagers again dug up such graves and threw the bodies into rivers, bogs, ravines and forests; the last trial he knows of was held in 1913 in Saratov province (pp. 353–354). Dates and cases are his; the chronicles and trial records were not seen for this edition. By his own time, he writes, villages cared less about the method of burial than about the place: people objected to burial in the common cemeteries, which they held clean and sacred, the shared property of the ancestors, who would not want such neighbours. The drunkards among the unclean dead were believed to suck the moisture from the earth around their graves, which people used to explain drought (p. 354).
T · Ust-Tsilma: the informants’ own list

T / UST-TSILMA Ust-Tsilma: the informants’ own list T. I. Dronova’s 2024 article rests on interviews and observation at funerals among Russian Old Believers without priests in the Ust-Tsilma district of the Komi Republic, on family manuscripts, and on laments held in the archive of the Komi Scientific Centre. It lists whom the community counts as ‘unclean’ dead: those who died unbaptised; suicides (hanged, shot, drowned); women who died in childbirth; stillborn children; sorcerers; missing persons whose bodies were not buried, soldiers excepted; those killed in peacetime; those struck by lightning; those drowned in unclear circumstances; and those who died in the bathhouse (p. 202). The ‘clean’ are those who died old, baptised infants and youths, those who died early but had made confession, and those killed in war, counted as martyrs. The words she records for the unnatural dead are samoubivets, visel’nik, zadavlennik, utoplennik and utopshoi; zalozhnyi does not occur in the text read (p. 201). The community’s teacher examines each suicide. Church rule forbids commemoration, but he asks whether the man was in health or ‘without mind’; in the second case the dead could be commemorated at common services and a funeral service held some years later, always with the stress that the death was ‘unclean’. Otherwise only the universal services of the parental weeks name them as ‘and those with them’, without their names, though alms may be given (pp. 202–203). The body was not to be touched with bare hands: it was dragged on hooks to a burial place outside the village, usually a low spot, and put in a pit into which went everything used, the rope, work mittens, the hook. People avoided that place. Suicides began to be buried in the cemeteries in the 1970s on the order of the village administration, which angered the Old Believers; many prayer-leaders held the cemeteries defiled, and some saw the ‘last times’ begin. Until recently such dead ‘dropped out’ of the memory of the living, and it was forbidden to speak their names; now families go to the cemetery and cense the graves but do not hold individual commemorations (p. 203). For an unbaptised child, if the parents’ neglect was the cause, the death counted as the parents’ sin to be confessed. Some held that such souls cannot find rest, others that they are spiritually blind but not sinful and wait in a ‘southern country’ that is not hell. Relatives watched the grave mound for forty days: if the earth stayed still, or rose, it was a sign of the child’s ‘pleasing to God’ state and a six-week requiem could be sung for him as ‘nameless’; if the mound sank, the child had been harmful to people while in the womb and was not commemorated (pp. 203–204). The Old Believers here are book-readers, and an informant answered from a patristic text on those who die suddenly and in water; the teacher’s answer on a man who falls through river ice was that every untimely death must be judged separately. This is one district, one researcher, informants whom she does not name, and a community that reads and weighs written church rules, so its list is an insider’s judgment, not evidence for any wider region (pp. 201–204).
T · Unbaptised and early dead children: what a Slavic survey allows for Russia

T / CHILDREN Unbaptised and early dead children: what a Slavic survey allows for Russia Irina Sedakova’s 2020 article in Folklore 80 surveys the death and funeral of a child across the Slavic world from archive and field data of the late nineteenth to mid-twentieth century. She says that her own records come mainly from Bulgarians in Bulgaria and in diaspora (p. 48). Almost all of what follows is therefore Slavic or Bulgarian, and only a few lines are attributed to Russian places. Her general statement is that a child who died without baptism and a name was thought to go to hell ‘as if not born’, and that the belief that such children become evil spirits is widespread. She lists the burial places assigned to them (beneath the house, under a window, in the yard, under a tree) without separating the regions in the passage read (p. 56). For baptised children the Russian items are these: in the Russian North a thread as long as the father’s or mother’s height was put in the coffin so that the dead child would not outgrow the parent and ‘walk’ (citing Listova 2001, p. 623); in the Vologda region an egg was put under the pillow of a small child (citing Vlasova 1999, p. 392) (p. 58). Russians, citing Naumenko 1998, p. 116, hold that a child of two or three becomes an angel and one of seven goes to heaven; the fate of an eight-year-old is judged by sins (pp. 61–62). These are second-hand citations to ethnographic compilations, and the article does not say which village or decade lies behind each. They are enough to show that the fear of the unbaptised dead was Russian as well as southern Slavic. They are not enough for a Russian map of child burial; for that the plate would need the primary regional records.
T · Two kinds of dead, and the acts that kept the unclean ones out

T / KEEPING THEM OUT Two kinds of dead, and the acts that kept the unclean ones out Svetlana Tolstaya divides the Slavic dead into two groups: the pure, who died a normal death and come back at fixed times without harming anyone, and the unclean (Russian zalozhnye), who died early or by violence, such as suicide, hanging or drowning, or who dealt with evil spirits in life. She adds that the dead of either kind might return because they were neglected, or because they worried about small children, and that the unclean visits were the ones guarded against (pp. 10–11). Her detailed protective measures come mostly from Polesie, which is not Russia: needle sewn right to left on the shroud, coffin carried out feet first through a side door or the window, a stone or branches on the grave, poppy seed and sand scattered for the dead to count until cockcrow, and the aspen stake (pp. 9–11). For the Russian North she gives one item: after the coffin was carried out, the floor was swept and the house washed, always towards the exit (p. 10). In the same passage she says that in different Slavic traditions the benches and tables were turned over and the water was poured out, and that East Slavs left inverted pots or bowls on graves; those lines are general and name no Russian place (p. 10). Her closing section adds a larger claim, that most characters of ‘lower mythology’ are the souls of such dead, a view she traces to Zelenin’s work on the rusalka (pp. 11–12). That last claim is disputed in the literature this atlas uses. Dynin, read for plate U, argues that the rusalka image is recent and composite and that Zelenin’s origin from the ‘pledged’ dead explains only part of it. The sentence on the plate therefore stays at what Tolstaya says about the dead, and not at what the figures of folk demonology ‘really’ are.
T · What Maksimov wrote about suicides and the drowned

T / A COLLECTOR, 1903 What Maksimov wrote about suicides and the drowned Sergei Maksimov’s Nechistaia, nevedomaia i krestnaia sila, published in 1903 by Prince Tenishev’s Ethnographic Bureau after Maksimov’s death, is a general book on spirits by a writer and collector; it gives few sources for individual items and the editors say they completed the manuscript. It is used here for statements that are short and concrete, not as a survey of practice. On suicides he writes that pious and strict people judged one who laid hands on himself to be ‘the devil’s ram’ (chertu baran), and that the drowned and the hanged were buried, where possible, on the very spot where they had committed the sin, in a bare mound, without a cross and outside the cemetery fence, ‘so that they fall more surely into the power of the unclean’ (pp. 16–17, as marked in the online copy of the 1994 reprint). On water, he says that bruises and scratches on a drowned body showed that the person had been in the vodyanoi’s paws, and that to find a body one set a wooden bowl with three wax candles afloat, and it stopped over the place (pp. 77–78, 83–84). On the wandering of such souls he adds that the girls who died by suicide cannot turn back from the state of a rusalka, and that children smothered by their mothers in sleep passed to the ‘secret people’ and were counted lost unless the mother saved them by forty days of prayer and strict fasting (pp. 20–21, 89). The three items agree with what the plate gets from Zelenin, Dronova and Tolstaya: a burial away from the churchyard for the self-killed and the belief that the water kept its dead. They add no place and no informant, so each is evidence for what an educated collector of the 1890s held to be the common belief, and not for a named village. Barsov, writing about the Olonets North in 1872, records that miscarried and unbaptised children were buried outside the cemetery fence in a swamp, and sometimes under the floor of the house; that a suicide in Voezersky parish, Kargopol district, was buried five versts from the church, where passers-by usually laid stones or sticks, burning the sticks when many had gathered (a footnote credits this report to L. Malinovsky); and that those who had hanged themselves in Andoma were buried on a hill among fir trees, face down (pp. 312–313). These are two or three places, not a map, and the Church did not prescribe the acts. They match in kind what the plate has from other regions: a site apart, stones or sticks left by passers-by, a turned body.
T · Walking dead and literary vampires

T / 04 Walking dead and literary vampires Ovseichik cites nineteenth- and early twentieth-century accounts (Dobrovolsky, Bogdanovich) that dead sorcerers walked, killed people and drank their blood, and adds, after Vinogradova and Levkievskaya, that such stories are rare in the East Slavic area and more typical of South Slavic vampire lore. The borderland material is mostly about where and how the impure dead were buried, not about what they did once they rose. The upyr’ of nineteenth-century Russian fiction is another matter. One thesis abstract places the literary vampire as a device used in Russian writing from the eighteenth century on, built on older belief. The atlas keeps the two apart: the field records read for this plate do not describe a figure like the literary vampire, and nothing here is evidence for one.

T / 05 Zelenin and his critics Zelenin’s 1916 compilation gathered reports from many provinces under one heading and read them together as a single belief: that the earth does not accept the dead of ‘unnatural’ death, who therefore stay among the living. He tied the category to the rusalki. The sources read for this plate raise three objections. Ovseichik will not extend the word ‘zalozhnye’ beyond its Vyatka use, because it is absent from Belarusian and other traditions and because burial methods varied. Avdeev, from epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs, argues that the related superstitions are of Christian times and not pagan survivals; only his abstract was read. Baiburin’s critique of reading rites as survivals of an earlier religion is a general objection to the method, not a verdict on Zelenin’s evidence. What remains usable is the dated record. The local reports in the compilation, such as the ravine burials on plate N and the Semik citations on plate O, are evidence of what someone wrote down, from whom and where. The unifying belief is Zelenin’s construction. Where the record is read here, it is cited by place.
T · A dispute about where the rule came from

T / 06 A dispute about where the rule came from Ethnographers of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries took such burial customs for pagan survivals. A. Avdeev argues the opposite for Muscovite Russia: from sixteenth to early eighteenth-century epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs he finds no obstacle to cemetery burial or regular commemoration of those who died violent deaths, and he holds that the related superstitions arose in Christian times. This plate has the abstract only. It cannot say how strong Avdeev’s evidence is or how far his conclusion reaches beyond the Muscovite sources. It is placed here so that the pagan-survival reading is not left standing alone.

T / 07 A rule remembered, 2018–2019 A. Ryko’s fieldwork in the Khislavichi district of the Smolensk region found only remnants of such beliefs. Informants born in the 1930s remember that those who hanged or drowned themselves were not taken to the common cemetery; younger people say they know nothing of it and that the drowned lay in the cemetery. Unbaptised infants were not counted as ‘unclean’ there. No one now says that certain dead can return and harm the living. Set beside Ovseichik, the two studies cover neighbouring districts and different decades of the same century, and they do not agree on unbaptised children. The author says the findings rest on memory and that it is not clear whether the trend is local.

PART I · THE CHURCH The Church’s own list In a church instructional text, Hieromonk Job (Gumerov) names the Saturdays on which the Church commemorates the dead: Meat Fare Saturday, the second, third and fourth Saturdays of Great Lent, Trinity Saturday and St. Demetrius Saturday. He explains the choice of Saturday by its place as the day of rest, and says the Lenten Saturdays stand in for the daily memorial services that are suspended during the fast. He gives St. Demetrius Saturday a precise origin: it was set up after the battle of Kulikovo in 1380, with the blessing of Sergius of Radonezh, first for the soldiers who fell and later for all the departed. This is the Church’s account of itself, written by a churchman; it is evidence for what the Church holds, not for what a village did. In Russian village tradition, the universal Saturdays formed an organic seasonal cycle of communion with the ancestral collective (roditeli) (Kremleva 1999, pp. 530–532). On Meat Fare Saturday (spring threshold) and Dmitrievskaya Saturday (autumn threshold), families observed dedicated meals: bliny, hot beer, and pork or mutton pies were served, and the first portion was set aside on the windowsill with the invitation 'Parents, come eat and drink with us'. At the cemetery on Trinity Saturday, graves were ritually swept with fresh birch brooms, and dyed eggs and pies were broken over the turf to share feast-food directly with the dead.
U · A day counted from Easter

PART II · WHY THE DAYS MOVE A day counted from Easter Easter moves from year to year, and the days of commemoration counted from it move with it. A source that says ‘Radonitsa’ or ‘Semik’ is giving a weekday and a week after Easter, not a date of the month. The Church now places Radonitsa on the Tuesday of Thomas week, the ninth day after Easter; that was 14 May in 2024. A reference work of 1913 describes it as falling mostly on the Monday of that week and in some places on the Tuesday, so the day itself varied by place. Semik is the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter. Counting Easter Sunday as day 0, that is day 46, and Trinity Saturday (day 48) falls two days later; the counting is this plate’s arithmetic, not a statement in the sources. Semik has no place in the Church’s calendar, which is why Maltsev’s Komi-Permyak material and the encyclopedia treat it as a folk day. Julian and Gregorian reckoning add a second layer: a family’s date for the same day can differ from the date in a modern table. This plate gives no dates for any year.
U · A day the church calendar does not have

PART III · REGIONAL: THE KOMI-PERMYAKS A day the church calendar does not have G. I. Maltsev records the commemoration days of the Komi-Permyaks: Radonitsa, Semik, Trinity Saturday, and the Saturdays before Pokrov and St. Demetrius. He writes that Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, is absent from the Orthodox calendar, that priests took no part in it in the late nineteenth century and did from the early twentieth. After Zelenin he reports that those dead by unnatural death were commemorated at Semik, and quotes a Kungur saying that they are deaf and blind except on that day. He also describes a slow move: the Permyaks began to hold this commemoration on the Saturdays of general remembrance, reasoning that prayers would be heard better then. His material is four recordings by one researcher, from a people who are not Russian. The plate uses it only as a regional comparison for a pattern that Russian sources describe. Read more fully, Maltsev’s article gives Semik among the Permyaks the name dzollun or sharlun and describes it as the day on which those who died unnatural deaths were commemorated, traditionally at the cemetery; for suicides, food was also set at home on a water barrel or on the threshold. Offerings named elsewhere in the article include pancakes and buns taken to graves in a report from Uzhum, afterwards given to the clergy, and pies, eggs and pancakes sent to the other world through a beggar or a river among Permyaks. Priests joined in the early twentieth century (a litia and censing of graves is cited from 1904), and today a memorial service for all the departed is held on Semik in the Svyato-Stefanovsky deanery of the Kudymkar diocese. The article rests on published sources, on material from the Kungur and Komi Zyuzda districts, and on the author’s own fieldwork in the Yusva, Gayny and Kosa districts between 1995 and 2016.

Chesnokova’s fieldwork in the Kostroma and Vladimir regions found the main cemetery commemoration falling in either the Easter or the Trinity period, and she says this corresponds broadly to certain regional zones, which the abstract does not name. Within the period one day carries the main rites, and she divides it into a preparation, a meeting of relatives at the cemetery, a walk among the graves, commemoration at the grave, and a continuation at home. She finds these days both family occasions and social ones, with their importance held or growing, and says collective commemoration repairs ties weakened by distance and broken family traditions. The abstract does not name the day, and the counts of respondents are not given.

U · Burying the rusalka at Bolshaya Vereika

PART IV · A FIELD RECORD Burying the rusalka at Bolshaya Vereika In the village of Bolshaya Vereika, Zemlyansk district, Voronezh oblast, women and girls ‘led’ or ‘buried’ a rusalka each year. N. P. Grinkova collected the rite twice, in 1925 and in July 1936, mainly from the storyteller A. K. Baryshnikova, who directed it in performance; she also acquired the figure and its props for the State Museum of Ethnography (collection no. 5866, 1936). The figure was a sheaf of reed (kuga), less often of straw, about a metre high, with cross-stalks for arms, a white cloth for a face, and a woman’s embroidered shirt, skirt and headscarf. It lay on a stretcher under a white cloth and three embroidered towels, so that only the head showed, like a dead woman laid out. The procession set out from the house where the figure was dressed, in holiday clothes, with reed stems for candles. One woman took the part of the priest: hair loose, a mat over her shoulders for a chasuble, and a worn bast shoe swung as a censer. She led a dance-tune song through the village and the others took up the refrain. In the rye field the figure was stripped, the towels and ribbons removed, and figure and stretcher poles thrown into the ditch at the field’s edge. The day was the zagovenye after Trinity, the last Sunday before the Apostles’ Fast. Baryshnikova gave two reasons: thrown into the rye, the rusalka makes the bread grow better; and the rite protects from rusalkas, who would frighten people all summer if it were not done. Women of the older generation took it seriously, and before 1917 the estate steward let women off work for it. The women said it was last done in 1935; in spring 1936 ‘somehow they did not gather’, and in July 1936 Grinkova saw only a staged reconstruction. The comparisons and the frame are Grinkova’s own: she places the rite among ‘burials of Kostroma’ and the cuckoo, cites Zelenin’s records of rusalka processions in Serdobsk district (Saratov province) and in Ryazan province, and reads all of them as survivals of a dying-and-resurrecting deity cult after Frazer. That interpretation is not adopted here. The record itself is a single village, recorded by one ethnographer from one main informant (pp. 178–181).
U · The rusalka: a southern name that reached the North late

U / THE RUSALKA The rusalka: a southern name that reached the North late Vladimir Dynin’s 1994 article in Etnograficheskoe obozrenie sets out how the East Slavs described the rusalka, using published provincial reports of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and recent expedition notes. In the south of Russia, in Ukraine and in part of Belarus she is mostly a young, beautiful girl with loose, long hair, and she is usually the soul of a drowned woman or of a child who died unbaptised; these are the places linked to the Trinity–Semik season and the rites of ‘seeing off’ the rusalka. In the Russian North, he says, the same word was not known until recently: correspondents of Tenishev from northern provinces said so, and Zelenin showed that it arrived there in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with town culture. Northern informants described a shaggy woman with long hanging breasts who combs her hair on a rock or a snag and who is called by other names: vodyanikha, chertovka, leshachikha. One recorded remark from the Kholmogory district runs that ‘now they call them rusalki, and before it was all chert’ (pp. 112–113). His conclusions are that the figure is missing from northern demonology, that it was still unsettled in the south, and that the earliest reports of the rusalka as such date from the eighteenth century. He therefore holds that the image is recent and was built from several beings: poludnitsy, wood and water spirits, and the dead honoured in ‘rusalia’ week. He derives the name from rusalia, a term he links to the Roman Rosalia memorial rite, and he adds that the cult of the ‘pledged’ dead, as Zelenin noted, spread widely in the eighteenth to twentieth centuries (pp. 113–114, 117–118). This is one side of an open argument. Dynin himself lists others who took the rusalka as an ancient nature spirit, as the dead ancestors, or as a female deity of moisture, and he says that none of these views has been generally accepted (p. 111). The plate therefore uses the article for what it records about regions and names, and treats the late-origin thesis as contested. Pages are taken from the running heads of the supplied PDF.
