V · Two aims, and the acts that serve them

V / 01 Two aims, and the acts that serve them An encyclopedia article on East Slavic funeral rites says the rite works in two directions: some acts help the dead reach the other world, others protect the living from the dead. Its protective and cleansing acts include washing the house after the coffin is carried out, turning objects over, covering mirrors and washing hands on returning from the cemetery. Its prohibitions include close relatives making the coffin and bringing food back from the cemetery. The explanation the article gives is general: the dead can harm the living, and the boundary between worlds stays open from the death until the burial and the fortieth day. It does not give a reason for each separate act, and it does not date its examples. The page does not name an author. The page has no bibliography, but it names its authorities in the text: Baiburin (1993), Razumova (2012), Tolstaya (2009, 2019), Spassky (1877) and an 1890 collection of materials on daily life. Washing as removal of the marks of the living is attributed to Baiburin; the epistolary character of laments in the Russian North to Tolstaya. Barsov (1872, p. 312) lists acts done so as not to fear the dead: touching the dead man’s heels, kissing him hard at the farewell, looking at the legs of the horse that carries him from under the shafts on the way to the cemetery, touching the house stove with the fingers on returning, and, if he still disturbs the living with apparitions, driving him off with a bridle on the Svir. He gives them as known customs from different places, not as one rite, and attaches no reason to any act beyond the stated aim. He adds that when someone dies without repentance, his relatives bow at the feet of everyone who comes to church, and sometimes of anyone they meet within two or three weeks, asking forgiveness of the dead person’s sins, in the belief that the sins pass to the living who take part in the singing or are bowed to; and that some Kargopol parishes have no custom of commemoration at all, with a saying that one does not stir a dead bone.

V / 02 In the house J. Rouhier-Willoughby, in a review of urban funerals, lists what the older village rite is reported to have included: candles lit, all the mirrors in the house covered, all water thrown out. She cites the ethnographers for covering the mirrors so that the soul would not be trapped, for discarding the water because it could trap the soul, and for mirrors being seen as symbolically like water because they reflect. The women who washed the body turned tables and benches over before washing them, she writes, so that death would enter the soil; a priest might also say a prayer of purification once the body had been carried out. She draws these from earlier ethnographers, so the village custom reaches the atlas at second hand. For the urban twentieth century she reports that the covering of shiny surfaces continued.

V / 03 Washing Washing the body appears in both sources as an obligatory part of the rite. The encyclopedia cites a scholar who argues that the strictness of the rule points to a purpose beyond cleaning: removing what marked the person as living. In the Russian North, it says, the washing was done by specially invited people, usually women past childbearing age. In the Khislavichi district of Smolensk, A. Ryko’s informants said neighbours were invited to wash, women washing women and men washing men, and she found no stated ban on relatives taking part. The encyclopedia’s prohibition concerns making the coffin, not washing; Ryko’s article names no ban on relatives for washing, and says that excluding close relatives would fit the general boundary function of washing, as a wider pattern and not as a rule recorded locally. The two sources describe different places and cannot be added together.
V · A 1927 survey: what was done in the house

V / 04 A 1927 survey: what was done in the house Zelenin’s survey of East Slavic ethnography (1927), § 132, lists the acts around a death. At the moment of death a vessel of water was set beside the dying person; many said they had seen the water stir, as if from the bathing of the soul that had just left. It stood on the table or windowsill for forty days, and people held that during that time the soul had not yet gone to the other world, and some that it drank the water. At the same moment the stove flues or a small window were opened and a cloth or towel hung out of the window. People explained the cloth in different ways: the soul dries itself on it, wipes its tears with it, or rests on it. Zelenin suggests it first eased the soul’s way out of the house and back. A long death agony was put down to dealings with unclean power, and then the roof ridge was broken or a ceiling board lifted so that the soul could leave. Copper coins were laid on the eyes so that the dead should not look at a member of the family, who would then die. The bed on which someone had died was thrown out or put in the hen house for the cock to cleanse. When the coffin was brought in, everyone left the house, pregnant women above all; they also left when it was carried out and were not to wash the body, or their child would die. In Olonets province, he writes, citing Barsov, the coffin went out through the window so that the dead could not find the way back; it was carried feet first and struck three times on the threshold so that the dead would take leave of the old home. Water standing in the house at the moment of death was poured out, because the dead might have drunk it. A woman followed the procession with a bath broom, sweeping the floor to the threshold and sprinkling water, and the floor was then washed. Zelenin reads this as magic, not hygiene, and gives the informants’ wording: the water is poured ‘to wash away the dead man’s traces’. While the body lay in the house the floor was not swept, ‘so as not to sweep out the living’; afterwards the rubbish was swept toward the house, so that its people would stay. Rye and barley were thrown behind the procession and on the coffin ‘so that no one in the house dies again’. An axe or knife was struck on the bench where the dead had lain, ‘to cut off death’. Bread was not baked while the body was in the house, and no sowing or planting was allowed in the village until the burial, or the crops would not come up. Zelenin merges Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian material, and I have kept to the items he gives for Russians or the Russian North or leaves general. His details come from the archive of the Russian Geographical Society and from regional collectors, cited by volume and number; the archive files were not seen. He gives no dates. The passages read do not mention covering mirrors, so the mirror material on this plate rests on the three other sources.

V / 05 Done without an explanation Ryko writes that people in the borderland often perform funeral actions without being able to say what they are for, and that as the motives fade the sense of obligation fades with them. This is her observation of one district, based on informants’ memories, and she says it is unclear whether the trend is local. It matters here because the reasons attached to protective acts in the other sources are the reasons collected from or ascribed to people at particular times. They are not a fixed meaning that every act always carried.

V / 06 Why the mirror? Several reasons are on record for covering mirrors. A hieromonk, writing against the custom, reports that people said the soul should not be frightened by its reflection, or the dead should not frighten the family, or the soul might slip into the world behind the mirror, which he says the devil rules. Rouhier-Willoughby, reporting earlier ethnographers, gives the reason that the soul should not be trapped, and ties mirrors to water, which was also thrown out because it could trap the soul. These do not agree with each other and none is shown here to be the original. The church writer is hostile and gives the folk reasons in order to dismiss them. The atlas lists the reasons and leaves the meaning of the act unsettled. Ethnolinguistic field evidence gathered across Russian provinces (Tolstaya 1999, pp. 321–324) documents the underlying structural logic of covering mirrors. In peasant worldview, the mirror is an active, permeable boundary between this world and the otherworld. The primary fear recorded among informants is the 'doubling' of death (udvoenie smerti): if the corpse or any living household member is reflected, death will inevitably strike a second person in the home. Secondarily, the unquiet soul, wandering about the house during the initial forty days, is thought vulnerable to entrapment inside the glass matrix, unable to cross over. Looking into an uncovered mirror while a corpse remains in the house was subject to an absolute taboo, threatening sickness or immediate death.

V / 07 The Church’s position Hieromonk Dometian calls the covering of mirrors a folk custom with nothing in common with the Orthodox burial rite, and he says the same of overturning tables and chairs, which he calls pagan survivals. He also reports a belief that one must not look out of a window at a funeral procession, and he tells believers to take the blessing of a priest as their only guide. This is a polemical text of unstated date. It shows what the Church objects to, and by implication what was practised, but it is not a count of practice.

W · Novosibirsk: dated decisions, as reported

W / 01 Novosibirsk: dated decisions, as reported In a 2023 interview, E. Krasilnikova of Novosibirsk State Technical University dates a run of local decisions. A 1920 decision concerned cutting the grove at the cemetery. In 1929 the Voskresenskaya church was ordered closed, and in April 1930 a crowd of about a thousand protested and was dispersed by the militia. The old cemetery became a garden and later part of a park; the church went to the park administration, held a planetarium and burned in the 1970s. She places the start of such demolitions in Siberia in the mid-1920s. The interview states the dates as facts but cites no file or archive for them, so they stand here as the interviewee’s report.

W / 02 Barnaul and Omsk In her account two large cemeteries in Barnaul were destroyed in the 1930s, graves were opened in search of valuables, which she says a local government decree backed, and bones were left scattered. She calls Barnaul the most radical case in Siberia; that comparison is her judgement. Omsk went another way. She says its historic necropolis survived until the 1950s, was recorded and photographed by a museum director before its demolition, and in 2005 fragments of its stones were gathered into a memorial square. Novosibirsk has no comparable memorial, she adds.
W · Curbs on a Moscow embankment, 2019

W / 03 Curbs on a Moscow embankment, 2019 A. Minkin reports that gravestones were found used as curbs near the Estrada Theatre on Bersenevskaya Embankment while the curbs were being replaced. The photographs came from a municipal deputy who posted them online, and some stones still showed dates of birth and death. The construction department told the outlet that the work was not under its direction. He also recalls a similar case from 2011 on Bolshaya Polyanka. A second report, by BFM (17 October 2019), describes the same find as granite steps of the theatre, not curbs. It quotes A. Frolov of the Arkhnadzor council, who attributed one slab to the gravestone of Colonel Pyotr Beketov from the Novospassky Monastery and read the find as a trace of the clearing of old cemeteries in the 1930s. BFM adds that Arkhnadzor preferred to leave the slabs where they were found, while the city’s heritage department decided they did not belong at the theatre and had not yet said what would be done with them. The two reports differ on what the stones were used as, and the attribution of the slab is one preservationist’s statement, not an inspection record. The 2019 find is therefore known through a deputy’s photographs and an outlet’s report, not through an inspection record.
W · Claims with no document behind them

W / 04 Claims with no document behind them The same article quotes an architect, S. Tkachenko, who says that reuse of granite for roads was normal in the 1920s and 1930s, that many stone buildings were demolished in 1934 and the rubble used as metro filler or concrete. The state enterprise ‘Ritual’ is quoted as saying the practice was common, that many cemeteries were cleared in the first half of the twentieth century for the metro and roads, with curbs at Sokolniki, Tverskoy Boulevard and Novaya Basmannaya Street, and that unused slabs were crushed into rubble. No decision, order or archive is cited for any of this. The atlas keeps the statements and marks them UNVERIFIED: they are plausible, they come from named speakers, and they are not documented here.

W / 05 Why the cemeteries went The interview names several kinds of motive, which this plate groups into four, and which the interview does not itself list as four: ideological (shedding pre-revolutionary culture and building a socialist city), practical (neglected graves after the Civil War, typhus burials, no relatives left to tend them), symbolic (local notables buried there whom the new authorities saw no need to remember) and emotional (funerals used to mobilise people, revolutionary rites replacing religious ones). For Barnaul she also describes the search of graves for valuables, which the four groups do not cover. These are her interpretations of Siberian cases and are not sourced in the interview. The atlas lists them as one reading, and does not give them as the cause of abandoned cemeteries elsewhere, including the one in the photograph. Documented property histories and municipal renovation records explain the destruction of urban necropolises as an ideological and utilitarian program. During the early Soviet five-year plans of the 1930s, pre-revolutionary churchyards were re-zoned as 'unsanitary wastelands' and systematically converted into public 'parks of culture and recreation' (Novosibirsk Central Park, Moscow's Simonov and Lazarevskoe). Stone materials from dismantled tombs were requisitioned for industrial and architectural construction: polished labradorite, granite, and limestone grave markers were planed down and reused as municipal paving curbs, embankment retaining stones, and foundational revetments for Moscow Metro stations.

X / 01 More dead than living A. Sergeeva, R. Gerlit and H. Krcmar analysed 33 social networks and online services, surveyed 173 internet users and interviewed experts, taking Russia as their example (Jusletter IT, 27 May 2020, IRIS 2020 proceedings). Their abstract expects services to host more deceased than living users in the coming decades, accounts and data to persist, the deceased to keep receiving invitations and birthday greetings, and heirs to find it hard to identify all accounts and reach the data. X · A dissertation on mourning online

X / 02 A dissertation on mourning online Katerina Linden’s doctoral dissertation at Uppsala (defended 23 April 2021) studies online commemoration in Russia by virtual ethnography of three memorial sites: Last Address, on the victims of Soviet repression; a site on the victims of the Nord-Ost siege; and the online memorial network Forever with Us. She argues that online tools enable communal remembrance, that this has three sides (between the living and the dead, among mourners, and as motive for action), and that digitalisation may challenge a political culture of forgetting. She also argues that the ‘right to be forgotten’ is not necessarily the answer, because difficulty in forgetting online could help repair a broken memory culture. This is an argument within her theoretical framework. The atlas has the abstract and title page only (read in the open full text) and treats it as her claim.

X / 03 Avatars and grief Researchers from HSE University in Nizhny Novgorod, T. Khusyainov and E. Urusova, are reported as saying that digital footprints can support grief by sustaining a sense of connection, and that the same tools can raise anxiety, delay acceptance of loss and increase the risk of retraumatisation. They describe AI avatars of the dead, which can recreate voice and habits and can also produce errors, with a comparison to Frankenstein’s creature. The two effects are put forward together by the researchers themselves, and the atlas leaves both open. The plate has a university news item, not the article. The item does not discuss Russian law.
X · What platforms say they do

X / 04 What platforms say they do A news item reports that VKontakte marks or deletes the page of a dead user at the request of relatives, who send a photograph of the death certificate. If the page is kept, the words ‘Страница умершего человека’ appear in place of the last-visit time. The same item says that since 2011 a VK page could be kept unchanged or deleted, that Odnoklassniki adds a black ribbon or turns the photo black and white, and that Facebook lets a ‘keeper’ be named for the page and gives it a memorial status with the words ‘Светлая память’ by the name; it adds that Instagram has a similar system. This is a report of platform policy as of 26 November, which the item gives by day; the year, 2020, comes from a Belarusian outlet’s report of the same news, so the policy described is six years old. The platforms’ own help pages were not read, and rules of this kind change. What the item shows is that a page of the dead is a category the platform has made a procedure for, with a document as the key. Primary operational regulations from VKontakte (VK Help Center / Terms of Service) document the formal digital protocol governing Russian accounts. Upon the verified submission of a state death certificate and proof of direct kinship, the platform offers relatives two mutually exclusive options: permanent account deletion or conversion into a frozen memorial profile (pamiatnaia stranitsa). When memorialized, a permanent text badge ('The page of a deceased person') is pinned beside the user's name; private messaging, profile editing, and new wall publications are permanently locked to avert spam, trolling, or identity theft, while existing photographs, posts, and past correspondence remain accessible to friends as a static digital cenotaph.

Укатилося красное солнышко Funeral lament Petrozavodsk (recorded); Olonets province Barsov prints this as the first lament in the collection. It opens not with the deathbed but with the sun going down behind mountains, forests, clouds and stars; the dead man's departure is described as a cosmic disappearance before it is described as a household loss. The second movement turns to the widow's children: they will wander, knock at strangers' windows, and walk a road that is not wide or trodden. The formula «победная головушка» (poor, wretched woman) is a genre marker, not a personal epithet. Fedosova dictated her laments to Barsov in Petrozavodsk in 1867–68. Barsov notes that she dictated slowly and that he wrote down each word; the text is a transcription of a repertoire, not a recording of a funeral. The atlas prints the first fifteen lines. The following line in the printed text contains a dialect form whose sense is not certain, and the excerpt stops before it. Голубушка мила—сестрица! Funeral lament Selo Tverdilovo, Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province This is one of the few complete laments in Barsov's first volume. It was recorded in Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province, not in the Olonets North, and printed as No. XI. Barsov's register of performers (pp. 326–327) identifies the performer as Klavdiya Momokova, a peasant of Selo Tverdilovo; she learned to lament in the village as a girl and was living in Moscow when Barsov wrote. The text is short enough to print in full. The sister's lament moves from the dead woman's departure to «unknown guests» to the emptiness of the house, the survivor's loss of a «secret word» and «protection», and then to the invocation of wind, earth, coffin lid and shroud. The request that the dead sister rise and speak is a conventional motif. The closing line asks not for resurrection but for the grief to be shortened. The text is printed in the original pre-1918 orthography; line breaks and repetitions are retained. After the last line Barsov prints a footnote with a variant of about twenty lines for the passage on the winds, the earth and the shroud; the variant is not reproduced here. Little dove, my dear sister! Where have you gone and arrayed yourself, Where have you gone and made yourself ready? On what road, on what pathway, To what guests, unknown, Unknown and unwanted? You have arrayed yourself, made yourself ready For eternal life, without end. Without you, my dear sister, Now everything here is empty, quite empty, The wide tower has grown empty, In the wide courtyard; Without you, my dear sister, I am no worker, no labourer, I take upon myself every kind of thing, Both cold and hunger And great reproach; Little dove, my dear sister! You will not call out to me, will not speak to me, You will not appear to me in a dream, You will not show yourself to me awake; I have lost my firm thought, A secret word—not to be carried abroad, And my great protection. Rise up, you wild winds, With your fine little whirlwinds! Scatter the yellow sands, The yellow sands—the small stones! Open up, mother moist earth, Open, coffin lid, Unfold, fine white shroud! Собаки ихны костья не волочатъ-ли? Funeral lament for the unburied dead Lake Onega / Petrozavodsk The lament is spoken by a daughter who survived a storm on Lake Onega; her father and brother drowned. In this passage she describes what happens to those who die without confession and without burial: their bodies are not given to the earth, the wind wraps them, the sun warms them, snow falls on them, and the family has no grave to visit. The passage contrasts this death with the good death at home, on one's own bench, with priests and burial. The text is No. XVII in Barsov's first volume and comes from Fedosova's repertoire. Barsov prints the full lament, which includes the storm, the survival and the search for the bodies. The atlas prints lines 175–192 only. Собаки ихны костья не волочатъ-ли? Во тяжкихъ грѣхахъ—безъ покаянія, Они приняли смерётушку напрасную; Тѣлеса у ихъ пойдутъ безъ погребенія, Не приданы ко матушкѣ сырой землѣ; Призавіе буйнымъ вѣтрышкомъ, Призагріе краснымъ солнышкомъ, Западётъ тѣло снѣжечкомъ перистымъ; Не знаемъ мы побѣдныя головушки— Не умершей мы ихной тамъ могилушки! Лучше далъ бы Господь скорую смерётушку, На своей бѣлой, брусовой имъ на лавочкѣ, Во своемъ домѣ крестьянской-бы во жирушкѣ; Мы поповъ отцевъ вѣдь тутъ да попросили-бы, Въ Божью церковь посвященну мы сносили-бы, Честно-именно вѣдь ихъ похоронили-бы; Мы-бы знали, гдѣ могилушка умершая, На Владычной Божій праздничекъ сходили-бы,
On the Death of Prince Meshchersky · На смерть князя Мещерского

Глагол времён! металла звон! Philosophical ode St Petersburg Derzhavin wrote the ode in 1779 on the death of Prince Aleksandr Ivanovich Meshchersky (1713–1779), a courtier and friend. It is not a funeral lament and was not performed at a funeral. It is a literary meditation on time, death and the vanity of rank, written for the court and the printed page. The opening turns the sound of a clock into the voice of time and the approach of the grave. The images that follow—death as a reaper, the tomb as the leveler, the monarch and the prisoner as food for worms—belong to the eighteenth-century graveyard tradition and to Orthodox moral verse. The atlas prints the first sixteen lines; the poem continues for another seventy-two lines. It is evidence for elite literary culture, not for peasant ritual. The word of times! The clang of metal! Your terrible voice confounds me; Your groan calls me, calls me, Calls—and brings me nearer to the grave. Scarcely had I seen this light When death already gnashes its teeth, Flashes its scythe like lightning, And cuts my days like grass. Nothing escapes the fatal claws, No creature flees them; Monarch and prisoner are food for worms, The fury of the elements devours tombs; Time gapes to wipe away glory: As swift waters flow into the sea, So days and years flow into eternity; Greedy death swallows kingdoms. Глагол времён! металла звон! Твой страшный глас меня смущает; Зовёт меня, зовёт твой стон, Зовёт — и к гробу приближает. Едва увидел я сей свет, Уже зубами смерть скрежещет, Как молнией косою блещет, И дни мои, как злак, сечет. Ничто от роковых когтей, Никая тварь не убегает; Монарх и узник — снедь червей, Гробницы злость стихий снедает; Зияет время славу стерть: Как в море льются быстры воды, Так в вечность льются дни и годы; Глотает царства алчна смерть.
Whether I wander along noisy streets… · Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных…

Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных, Lyric poem Composed 1829; published in Literaturnaya gazeta, St Petersburg Pushkin wrote the poem on 26 December 1829; it was published in Literaturnaya gazeta on 6 January 1830. It is a lyric meditation, not a funeral text. The speaker moves through a street, a church, a crowd of youths, an oak, an infant, and ends at the entrance to the grave, where young life continues and indifferent nature shines. The poem is used in the plate on the grave because it states the grave as a place that is both personal («closer to my dear native place») and impersonal («it is all the same to the insensible body»). The «eternal vaults» are a literary image, not a description of a cemetery. The text follows the modern-spelling edition cited; the source page records the pre-reform variants. Whether I wander along noisy streets, Or enter a crowded church, Or sit among mad youths, I give myself up to my dreams. I say: the years will rush by, And however many of us are visible here, We shall all go down beneath the eternal vaults— And someone's hour is already near. Whether I look at a solitary oak, I think: the patriarch of the forests Will outlive my forgotten age, As he outlived the age of my fathers. Whether I caress a dear infant, I already think: farewell! I yield my place to you: It is time for me to decay, for you to bloom. Every day, every year I am accustomed to accompany with thought, Trying to guess among them The anniversary of my coming death. And where will fate send death to me? In battle, in wandering, in the waves? Or will the neighboring valley Receive my cooled ashes? And though it is all the same to the insensible body Where it decays, Still, closer to my dear native place I would like to rest. And let young life play At the entrance to the grave, And let indifferent nature Shine with eternal beauty. Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных, Вхожу ль во многолюдный храм, Сижу ль меж юношей безумных, Я предаюсь моим мечтам. Я говорю: промчатся годы, И сколько здесь ни видно нас, Мы все сойдём под вечны своды — И чей-нибудь уж близок час. Гляжу ль на дуб уединенный, Я мыслю: патриарх лесов Переживёт мой век забвенный, Как пережил он век отцов. Младенца ль милого ласкаю, Уже я думаю: прости! Тебе я место уступаю: Мне время тлеть, тебе цвести. День каждый, каждую годину Привык я думой провождать, Грядущей смерти годовщину Меж их стараясь угадать. И где мне смерть пошлёт судьбина? В бою ли, в странствии, в волнах? Или соседняя долина Мой примет охладелый прах? И хоть бесчувственному телу Равно повсюду истлевать, Но ближе к милому пределу Мне всё б хотелось почивать. И пусть у гробового входа Младая будет жизнь играть, И равнодушная природа Красою вечною сиять.
I come out alone onto the road… · Выхожу один я на дорогу…

Выхожу один я на дорогу; Lyric poem Composed 1841; published in Otechestvennye zapiski Lermontov wrote the poem in 1841, the year of his death; it was published in Otechestvennye zapiski in 1843. It is a lyric meditation, not a funeral text. The speaker is alone on a flinty road at night; he no longer expects anything from life and seeks freedom and peace, but he explicitly rejects the «cold sleep of the grave» in favour of a living, dreaming sleep. The poem is used in the plate on death in art because it imagines death as a threshold that is also a place of continuing life. The dark oak at the end is a literary image, not a cemetery custom. The text follows the 1989 edition cited. I come out alone onto the road; Through the mist the flinty path gleams. The night is still. The wilderness hearkens to God, And star speaks to star. In the heavens it is solemn and wondrous! The earth sleeps in a blue radiance... Why is it so painful and so hard for me? Am I waiting for something? Do I regret anything? I no longer expect anything from life, And I do not regret the past at all. I seek freedom and peace! I would like to forget myself and fall asleep! But not with that cold sleep of the grave... I would like to fall asleep like that forever, So that the powers of life might slumber in my breast, So that, breathing, my chest might rise quietly, So that, all night, all day, cherishing my hearing, A sweet voice might sing to me of love, So that above me, forever green, The dark oak might bend and murmur. Выхожу один я на дорогу; Сквозь туман кремнистый путь блестит. Ночь тиха. Пустыня внемлет богу, И звезда с звездою говорит. В небесах торжественно и чудно! Спит земля в сиянье голубом... Что же мне так больно и так трудно? Жду ль чего? Жалею ли о чем? Уж не жду от жизни ничего я, И не жаль мне прошлого ничуть. Я ищу свободы и покоя! Я б хотел забыться и заснуть! Но не тем холодным сном могилы... Я б желал навеки так заснуть, Чтоб в груди дремали жизни силы, Чтоб, дыша, вздымалась тихо грудь, Чтоб, всю ночь, весь день мой слух лелея, Про любовь мне сладкий голос пел, Надо мной чтоб, вечно зеленея, Темный дуб склонялся и шумел.
Hearing the horrors of war… · Внимая ужасам войны…

Внимая ужасам войны, Lyric poem Composed 1855; published 1856 Nekrasov wrote the poem in 1855, during the Crimean War, and published it in 1856. It is not a soldier's song or a funeral lament. It is a literary argument that the true grief of war belongs to mothers, whose tears cannot be consoled, while wives and friends forget. The poem is used in the plate on collective death as a counter to the state's monumental memory. It insists on the one mourner who does not forget, and it compares her to a weeping willow that cannot lift its branches. The «bloody field» is a literary generalization; the poem gives no place, date or name. Hearing the horrors of war, At each new victim of battle, I grieve not for the friend, not for the wife, I grieve not for the hero himself... Alas! the wife will be comforted, And the friend will be forgotten by his best friend; But somewhere there is one soul— It will remember until the grave! Amid our hypocritical deeds And all the vulgarity and prose, I have glimpsed in the world One kind of holy, sincere tears— The tears of poor mothers! They cannot forget their children, Perished on the bloody field, As a weeping willow cannot lift Its drooping branches... Внимая ужасам войны, При каждой новой жертве боя Мне жаль не друга, не жены, Мне жаль не самого героя… Увы! утешится жена, И друга лучший друг забудет; Но где-то есть душа одна — Она до гроба помнить будет! Средь лицемерных наших дел И всякой пошлости и прозы Одни я в мире подсмотрел Святые, искренние слёзы — То слезы бедных матерей! Им не забыть своих детей, Погибших на кровавой ниве, Как не поднять плакучей иве Своих поникнувших ветвей…
Frost, Red Nose (excerpt) · Мороз, Красный нос (отрывок)

Медлительно, важно, сурово Narrative poem Composed 1863–64; the poem is set in a Russian peasant village Frost, Red Nose (1863–64) is a narrative poem about the death of the peasant Prokl and the grief of his widow Daria. The excerpt describes the laying out of the body: the silence in the house, the candle at the head, the wide linen shirt, the new bast shoes, the calloused hands. Nekrasov drew on ethnographic material, and contemporaries read the poem as a picture of peasant life, but it is not a transcript of a ritual. The poem's funeral lament, which follows this passage, is Nekrasov's literary composition. The atlas does not present it as a folk lament; for recorded laments, see Plate G. The excerpt is printed as a literary image of the ritual, not as evidence of what was said or done. Slowly, gravely, sternly The sad work was done: No unnecessary word was spoken, No tears were shown outwardly. He has fallen asleep, having laboured in sweat! He has fallen asleep, having worked for the earth! He lies, untouched by care, On the white pine table, He lies motionless, stern, With a burning candle at his head, In a wide linen shirt And new linden bast shoes. His big, calloused hands, Which had lifted so much labour, His handsome face, untouched by torment— And a beard down to his hands... Медлительно, важно, сурово Печальное дело велось: Не сказано лишнего слова, Наружу не выдано слез. Уснул, потрудившийся в поте! Уснул, поработав земле! Лежит, непричастный заботе, На белом сосновом столе, Лежит неподвижный, суровой, С горящей свечой в головах, В широкой рубахе холщовой И в липовых новых лаптях. Большие, с мозолями руки, Подъявшие много труда, Красивое, чуждое муки Лицо — и до рук борода…
Inscription on the tomb of A. V. Suvorov · Надпись на надгробии А. В. Суворова

Здесь лежит Суворов. Epitaph / gravestone inscription Annunciation Church, Alexander Nevsky Lavra Suvorov died in 1800 and was buried in the Annunciation Church of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra in St Petersburg. The slab carries only these three words. The attribution to Derzhavin rests on an anecdote recorded in the commentary to Nikolai Gnedich's poem «Inscription to Suvorov's Tomb»: Suvorov asked Derzhavin what epitaph he would write, and Derzhavin replied that three words were enough. The original slab was later replaced by a longer one with titles, but Suvorov's wish prevailed and the simple inscription was restored. The atlas prints the inscription as an inscription, not as a poem. The exact history of the slab is summarized in the Lavra and museum notices cited. Here lies Suvorov. Здесь лежит Суворов.
Funeral sticheron: «I weep and lament…» · Стихира на погребении: «Плачу и рыдаю…»

Плачу и рыдаю, Liturgical chant (sticheron) Russian Orthodox funeral rite for the laity This sticheron, Tone 8, is sung in the Orthodox funeral rite for the laity. It is not a folk lament and was not composed for a village performance; it is the Church's own funeral language. The text is attributed to John of Damascus (c. 676–749) and is received in the Slavonic funeral rite. The sticheron states the paradox the plate discusses: the human person is created in the image of God and is nevertheless disfigured in the grave, and this is a «mystery» ordained by God, not a defeat of the creator. The English translation is the atlas's own; it follows the Church Slavonic text, not a modern Russian translation. I weep and lament when I think of death, and see lying in the tombs our beauty, created in the image of God, disfigured, without glory, without form. O wonder! What is this mystery that has come upon us? How have we been given over to corruption? How have we been joined to death? Truly, by the command of God, as it is written, who grants rest to the departed. Плачу и рыдаю, егда помышляю смерть, и вижду во гробех лежащую по образу Божию созданную нашу красоту, безобразну, безславну, не имущую вида. О, чудесе! Что сие еже о нас бысть таинство? Како предахомся тлению? Како сопрягохомся смерти? Воистинну Бога повелением, якоже писано есть, подающаго преставльшемуся упокоение.
The steppe, and steppe all around · Степь да степь кругом

Кони мчат-несут, Literary song / folk song Surikov's poem was written in 1869 and revised in 1877. It became one of the most widely sung Russian songs about a death on the road: a coachman dying in the steppe gives his comrade instructions for burial, for the horses, for his parents and for his young wife. The poem does not name a province; the ‘Mozdok steppe’ locates it in the North Caucasus, on the road, not in a village. The song is literary in origin, not a recorded folk lament. Its instructions — bury me here, take the horses home, tell my wife not to wait — are close to the formulas of a death on the road, but they are Surikov's composition. Use it as a literary song, not as a transcript of a peasant funeral. The horses race and carry me on, The steppe runs far away; The snowy storm Hums over the steppe. Snow and snow all around; Grief takes the heart; Of the Mozdok Steppe the coachman sings… How wide and great The steppe's expanse; How in the deaf steppe A coachman was dying; How in his last Hour before death He gave his command To his comrade: “I see death will strike me Here, in the steppe— Do not remember, friend, My evil offences. My evil offences, And my follies, Unreasonable words, Former rudeness. Bury me Here, in the deaf steppe; Take my black horses Home. Take them home, Give them to my father; Carry a bow To my old mother. To my young wife You say, my friend, That she should not wait For me at home… By the way, do not forget To tell her: It is hard for me to leave her A widow! Give her a parting word, A word of farewell, And give her the ring, The betrothal ring. Let her not grieve for me; Let her not be sad; With the one her heart loves, Let her be married!” The coachman fell silent, A tear rolls… And in the deaf steppe The snowstorm weeps. It wails, A groan stands in the steppe, The same song in it Sounds of the coachman: “How wide and great The steppe's expanse; How in the deaf steppe A coachman was dying.” Кони мчат-несут, Степь всё вдаль бежит; Вьюга снежная На степи гудит. Снег да снег кругом; Сердце грусть берет; Про моздокскую Степь ямщик поет… Как простор степной Широко-велик; Как в степи глухой Умирал ямщик; Как в последний свой Передсмертный час Он товарищу Отдавал приказ: «Вижу, смерть меня Здесь, в степи, сразит, — Не попомни, друг, Злых моих обид. Злых моих обид, Да и глупостей, Неразумных слов, Прежней грубости. Схорони меня Здесь, в степи глухой; Вороных коней Отведи домой. Отведи домой, Сдай их батюшке; Отнеси поклон Старой матушке. Молодой жене Ты скажи, друг мой, Чтоб меня она Не ждала домой… Кстати ей ещё Не забудь сказать: Тяжело вдовой Мне её кидать! Передай словцо Ей прощальное И отдай кольцо Обручальное. Пусть о мне она Не печалится; С тем, кто по сердцу, Обвенчается!» Замолчал ямщик, Слеза катится… А в степи глухой Вьюга плачется. Голосит она, В степи стон стоит, Та же песня в ней Ямщика звучит: «Как простор степной Широко-велик; Как в степи глухой Умирал ямщик».
From behind the island, into the reach · Из-за острова на стрежень

Из-за острова на стрежень, Literary song / folk song Sadovnikov's poem was published in 1883 and became a folk song in the 1890s. It retells an episode from Kostomarov's study of Stenka Razin: the ataman throws his captive Persian princess into the Volga to stop his men's mockery. The last line is a command to sing ‘for the repose of her soul’ — a memorial formula used over a woman who has just been drowned. The poem is literary, not a recorded song. It uses the river as a grave and the chorus as a memorial. It is relevant to the water plate and to the plates on the returning dead, but it is not evidence for a ritual. The ‘Persian princess’ is a literary figure; the poem gives no source for her. From behind the island, into the reach, Onto the broad river wave, Out run the painted, Sharp-prowed boats. In the front boat Stenka Razin, Embracing his princess, Celebrates a new wedding, Merry and drunk. And the princess, lowering her eyes, Neither alive nor dead, Timidly listens to the drunken, Unreasonable words. “I will spare nothing! I will give my wild head!”— It rings over the surrounding… Banks and islands. “Look, brothers, the ataman Has traded us for a woman! He spent a night with her— By morning he has become a woman… He has gone mad…” The mockery, the whisper The drunken ataman hears— The captive Persian woman He embraces more tightly, her full waist; His eyes filled angrily with blood, The ataman’s eyes, His black brows lowered, A storm is gathering. “Eh, my native nurse, Volga, mother-river! You have not seen gifts From a Don Cossack!.. So that there be no shame Before free people, Before the free river— Here, nurse… take her!” With a mighty swing he lifts The captive princess And, without looking, throws her Into the onrushing wave… “Why have you fallen silent, brave ones?.. Hey, Frolka-devil, dance!.. Strike up, lads, a chorus For the repose of her soul!..” Из-за острова на стрежень, На простор речной волны Выбегают расписные, Острогрудые челны. На переднем Стенька Разин, Обнявшись с своей княжной, Свадьбу новую справляет И веселый и хмельной. А княжна, склонивши очи, Ни жива и ни мертва, Робко слушает хмельные, Неразумные слова. «Ничего не пожалею! Буйну голову отдам!» — Раздается по окрестным… Берегам и островам. «Ишь ты, братцы, атаман-то Нас на бабу променял! Ночку с нею повозился — Сам наутро бабой стал… Ошалел…» Насмешки, шепот Слышит пьяный атаман — Персиянки полоненной Крепче обнял полный стан; Гневно кровью налилися Атамановы глаза, Брови черные нависли, Собирается гроза. «Эх, кормилица родная, Волга, матушка-река! Не видала ты подарков От донского казака!.. Чтобы не было зазорно Перед вольными людьми, Перед вольною рекою, — На, кормилица… возьми!» Мощным взмахом поднимает Полоненную княжну И, не глядя, прочь кидает В набежавшую волну… «Что затихли, удалые?.. Эй ты, Фролка-черт, пляши!.. Грянь, ребята, хоровую За помин ее души!..»
Along the wild steppes of Transbaikalia · По диким степям Забайкалья

По диким степям Забайкалья, Folk song / convict song A convict song known in many variants. The text printed here follows the pre-1929 songbook version; the 1950 Leningrad collection is cited for the song's later recorded form. The plot is a return: a man escapes across Baikal, meets his mother, and learns that his father is dead and his brother is in Siberia. The grave is not shown; it is reported in speech. The song is relevant to the plates on roads, vanished villages and the empty house, but it is not a funeral text. It shows how the grave enters a family narrative at the moment of return. The ‘truth’ for which the prisoner suffered is a literary-political formula, not a documented charge. Along the wild steppes of Transbaikalia, Where they dig gold in the mountains, A vagrant, cursing his fate, Dragged himself with a sack on his shoulders. He walks through the dense taiga, Where only the little birds sing, His kettle troubles his side, Dry leather shoes beat his feet. On him a poor shirt With many different patches, A convict's cap on him And a grey prison robe. He fled from prison on a dark night, In prison he suffered for the truth— He can go no further, Lake Baikal spread before him. The vagrant approaches Baikal, Takes a fisherman's boat And begins a sad song— About his homeland he sings: “I left my young wife, I left my little children, Now I go at random, God knows whether I shall see her!” The vagrant crossed Baikal, His dear mother comes to meet him. “Ah, hello, hello, mother, Is father well, I want to know?” “Your father has long been in the grave, Buried in the damp earth, And your brother has long been in Siberia, Long has he rattled his chains. Let us go, let us go, my son, Let us go to our native hut, Your wife there pines for her husband, And the children weep in a crowd.” По диким степям Забайкалья, Где золото роют в горах, Бродяга, судьбу проклиная, Тащился с сумой на плечах. Идет он густою тайгою, Где пташки одни лишь поют, Котел его сбоку тревожит, Сухие коты ноги бьют. На нем рубашонка худая Со множеством разных заплат, Шапчонка на нем арестанта И серый тюремный халат. Бежал из тюрьмы темной ночью, В тюрьме он за правду страдал — Идти дальше нет больше мочи, Пред ним расстилался Байкал. Бродяга к Байкалу подходит, Рыбацкую лодку берет И грустную песню заводит — Про родину что-то поет: «Оставил жену молодую, Оставил я малых детей, Теперь я иду наудачу, Бог знает, увижусь ли с ней!» Бродяга Байкал переехал, Навстречу родимая мать. «Ах, здравствуй, ах, здравствуй, мамаша, Здоров ли отец, хочу знать?» — «Отец твой давно уж в могиле, Сырою землею зарыт, А брат твой давно уж в Сибири, Давно кандалами гремит. Пойдем же, пойдем, мой сыночек, Пойдем же в курень наш родной, Жена там по мужу скучает, И плачут детишки гурьбой».

Чёрный ворон, чёрный ворон, Folk song / Cossack song A Cossack song about a wounded man who answers the raven circling over him. The first three stanzas refuse the bird its prey; the last accepts it. The ‘marriage’ is to an arrow in battle, and the bloody handkerchief is to be carried to the beloved. The song is built on a single address and a reversal, not on a narrative. The literary source is usually identified as Veryovkin's poem of 1831, but the text printed here is a folk variant. The Wikisource page names no songbook. Use it as a song text, not as a record of a specific funeral; the raven is an image of death, not a belief. Black raven, black raven, Why do you circle above me? You will not get your prey, Black raven, I am not yours! You will not get your prey, Black raven, I am not yours! Why do you spread your claws Above my head? Do you think to make me your prey? Black raven, I am not yours! Do you think to make me your prey? Black raven, I am not yours! Carry the bloody handkerchief To my dear love. Tell her—she is free, I have married another. Tell her—she is free, I have married another. A tempered arrow married me In the midst of the fatal battle. I see my death is coming— Black raven, I am not yours! I see my death is coming— Black raven, I am all yours… Чёрный ворон, чёрный ворон, Что ты вьёшься надо мной? Ты добычи не дождёшься, Чёрный ворон, я не твой! Ты добычи не дождёшься, Чёрный ворон, я не твой! Что ж ты когти распускаешь Над моею головой? Иль добычу себе чаешь? Чёрный ворон, я не твой! Иль добычу себе чаешь? Чёрный ворон, я не твой! Отнеси платок кровавый К милой любушке моей. Ей скажи — она свободна, Я женился на другой. Ей скажи — она свободна, Я женился на другой. Калена стрела венчала Среди битвы роковой. 1380 · St. Demetrius Saturday is set up

After the battle of Kulikovo a Saturday of commemoration is instituted, first for the fallen soldiers and later for all the departed, with the blessing of Sergius of Radonezh. This is the Church’s own account of the origin, as a churchman tells it.

The Last Judgment icon from the Nativity monastery in Novgorod is painted in registers, with the saved and the damned arranged as populations. It is an image made to be read, and it will remain the basic model for Russian judgement pictures for centuries.
10 October 1723 · Peter I restricts burial inside towns

A decree orders that the overcrowded churchyard cemeteries be moved outside the city, with an exception for ‘notable persons’. Pravenc adds that it ordered raised tombs levelled; Rozanov puts that order in an earlier decree of 12 April 1722, and another article dates the burial decree 16 October. The date given here is Pravenc’s and Rozanov’s. After Peter’s death the churchyard burial resumes; the measure is a precedent more than a settlement.

Tens of thousands die. Grigorii Orlov is sent to Moscow with emergency powers; the dead are buried outside the city, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo begins with unnamed plague victims. Mass death produces the modern out-of-town cemetery.
1771 · Burial in communal pits is banned

The online encyclopedia entry on Semik says that unidentified and unclaimed bodies were once placed in open communal pits, skudelnitsy, and that Catherine II banned burial in them in 1771. The entry is anonymous and cites no decree.
An icon of the Last Judgment is painted in the Volga region, 180 × 137 cm. Its compartments and inscribed bands derive from printed engravings: the judgement has become a page.

Archbishop Veniamin’s handbook sets out the rationale for commemoration on the third, ninth and fortieth days: the Resurrection, the nine ranks of angels, the Ascension. It is the clearest statement of the scheme that later writers would call a folk custom.
The collection of Russian folktales on which a 2025 reading of Baba-Yaga’s hut as a threshold rests. The folktales are narrative, not a record of burial practice.
1865 · Perov paints Seeing Off the Dead

A small canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm, of a family carrying a coffin on a sled. The painting becomes a reference point for the representation of peasant death and is later connected by the gallery to Nekrasov’s poem of 1862–63.

Three volumes of laments recorded in the Olonets region (funeral laments in 1872, recruit and soldier laments in 1882, wedding laments in 1886) establish lament as a composed, performed genre with named performers and a repertoire. This is the moment the Russian lament becomes an archive.

An unknown photographer records a memorial meal at Smolensk cemetery in St Petersburg. It is one of the few nineteenth-century photographs in this atlas that shows the ritual meal rather than the monument.
Tolstoy’s novella turns the deathbed into a corridor. It is not an ethnographic document; it is evidence of how the educated Russian reader was invited to imagine dying.

D. K. Zelenin publishes his study of those who die an unnatural death and of the rusalki, and gives the category zalozhnye pokoiniki its lasting form. The book is a synthesis, and its category is an argument.

Revolution and civil war break the institutions that had produced most of the sources above: parishes, monasteries, consistories, the ethnographic collections of the imperial academies. After this point, the atlas’s sources change kind.
1925 · Moscow holds a design competition for a crematorium
The Moscow communal administration holds an architectural competition in 1925. The crematorium is later fitted into the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin at the Donskoy Monastery.

The crematorium opens in the church building at the Donskoy Monastery: 12 January 1927 in Sokolova’s account, a trial burning on 11 January on one hobbyist page. The official opening is 6 October 1927 (Memorial’s Topos database; 7 October on the hobbyist page).
1920–1930 · Novosibirsk: cemetery grove, church closure, protest

In the account of E. Krasilnikova, a 1920 decision concerned cutting the grove at the cemetery, the Voskresenskaya church was ordered closed in 1929, and in April 1930 a crowd of about a thousand protested and was dispersed by the militia. The old cemetery became a garden and later part of a park.

The destruction or truncation of monastic and parish burial grounds in the Soviet period is well attested in general terms, but it has not been itemised by this atlas. The record here is a gap, not a list.

In Krasilnikova’s account two large cemeteries in Barnaul were destroyed in the 1930s, graves were opened for valuables and remains left scattered. She calls Barnaul the most radical case in Siberia; that comparison is her judgement.
1935 · Malevich buried under a black square

The painter’s ashes are buried near Nemchinovka under an oak. A wooden cube with a black square, made by Suetin, marks the grave. By one newspaper account the oak is felled in 1941 and the grave is later lost.
1 August 1936 · Decree on resettlement from the flood zone

An article on Cherepovets district states that resettlement followed a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee and the Council of People’s Commissars of that date, and that the residents of about seven hundred villages and hamlets were moved out of the flood zone. The decree itself was not seen.
Hundreds of thousands die in Leningrad and are buried in mass graves that become the ground of the Piskaryovskoye memorial. The sites are administrative before they are sacred.
The ensemble by A. V. Vasil’ev and E. A. Levinson opens on the fifteenth anniversary of victory. The flame is carried from the Field of Mars, where it had been lit in 1957.
8 May 1967 · The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

The monument by Dmitrii Burdin, Vladimir Klimov and Iurii Rabaev, with the sculptor Nikolai Tomskii, opens at the Kremlin wall. An unmanageable number of war dead is converted into one body that can be visited.

The state monopoly on funeral services ends; commercial funeral homes, municipal fee schedules and, later, online memorials appear. Orthodoxy returns to public ritual. The atlas marks this period as under-researched rather than describing it as a unified new culture of death.
2005 · Omsk gathers fragments of its necropolis into a square

Krasilnikova says the historic necropolis of Omsk survived until the 1950s and was recorded and photographed by a museum director before its demolition. In 2005 fragments of its stones were gathered into a memorial square. Novosibirsk has no comparable memorial.
2010 · The census counts villages with no inhabitants

Press reports of the 2010 census figures put the number of villages that exist de jure but have no inhabitants at 19,400, up from 13,000, and say 36,200 villages have fewer than ten residents. The reports give figures, not the fate of the cemeteries.
2013–2021 · Roadside memorial signs counted on three highways

M. G. Matlin drives sections of three federal highways in the Middle Volga repeatedly and documents 299 roadside memorial signs, with dates of death from 1965 to 2019. He sorts them into a family that imitates the cemetery and one that does not.
2016–2017 · Fieldwork on cemetery commemoration in Kostroma and Vladimir
E. G. Chesnokova’s fieldwork finds the main cemetery commemoration falling in the Easter or the Trinity period, following regional zones. Only the abstract was read.
2018–2019 · Fieldwork in Khislavichi district, Smolensk region

A. Ryko records that informants born in the 1930s remember a ban on taking those who hanged or drowned themselves to the common cemetery, while younger people say they know nothing of it. Neighbours washed the dead, women washing women and men washing men. She says the findings rest on memory and that it is unclear whether the trend is local.
June 2019 · Domovoy beliefs recorded in Severny Kommunar

M. A. Granova records beliefs about the domovoy in Severny Kommunar, Sivinsky district, Perm Krai, and compares them with older university-archive material. She finds the beliefs much reduced and gives this as a tendency; the number of informants is not stated.
2019 · Gravestones found used as curbs on Bersenevskaya Embankment

A municipal deputy posts photographs of gravestones used as curbs near the Estrada Theatre in Moscow; some stones still show dates of birth and death. The construction department says the work was not under its direction. The find is known through the photographs and an outlet’s report, not through an inspection record.
2020 · A study of the digital afterlife of Russian internet users

A. Sergeeva, R. Gerlit and H. Krcmar analyse 33 social networks and online services, survey 173 users and interview experts. Their abstract expects services to host more deceased than living users in the coming decades. This is a projection; only the abstract was read.
2023 · Muon survey in the Pskov-Caves Monastery

A team lays nuclear-emulsion detectors in the caves at Pechory to image two objects with atmospheric muons. The newspaper account reports a hidden passage of about 12 m behind a walled crypt, a continuation of Trinity Street and a cavity of roughly 3 × 6 × 3 m. These are the team’s estimates as quoted, not checked by opening.

The container in which the body is carried and buried. Described in the ethnography as plain, made of planks, sometimes hollowed from a single trunk in northern accounts. By the late imperial period it is increasingly a purchased object. It appears in plate B as furniture, in plate C as the centre of the rite, and in plate J as the box that organises Perov’s painting.

The cross set on the grave; several formal types are recorded. Eight-pointed, six-pointed and four-pointed crosses are all found on Russian graves, with regional and period variation. The roofed cross (golubets) shelters the cross under a gable and turns the grave into a small building. The atlas draws four types as measured elevations and marks the drawings as reconstructions.

Lit at the funeral, at memorial services and at the grave. A small, expendable object with a long life in the sources: it marks the presence of prayer, it is placed in the hand or beside the body in some descriptions, and it is bought and carried by mourners. The atlas uses it as a graphic sign for the presence of ritual time.

The stone, cross or structure that identifies a grave. In the medieval and early modern period the marker might be a stone slab or a wooden cross; from the eighteenth century the monument becomes an architectural object with an inscription, a portrait or a symbol. The atlas keeps the marker and the grave separate: a grave can exist without a marker, and a marker can survive its grave.

Cloth that covers or wraps the body. Regionally variable in form and name: a shroud, a covering, a piece of linen. Its function is to separate the body from the hands that carry it and to present the dead as a figure rather than a corpse. The atlas does not illustrate a specific example because it has not verified one.

Bread, pancakes or grain preparations eaten at the memorial meal. Bread and bliny recur in descriptions of the memorial table; the grain dish kutya is the most explicitly ritual of the foods. The atlas treats the food as an object with a documented context and an undocumented prehistory.

Boiled grain sweetened with honey, eaten at memorial meals and blessed at memorial services. Wheat or rice, honey, later raisins. The church dish is called kolivo; household kutya may be richer. The grain is read as a figure of resurrection. The relationship between the two dishes is not settled by the sources used here.

The bowl, cup or dish reserved for the memorial meal or for the dead. A place is set for the dead in some accounts, with a cup or a portion. The object is unremarkable in itself; what makes it ritual is the reservation — it is not used for the living.

The formal entrance to a cemetery, with a wall and often a chapel. From the late eighteenth century the cemetery is a walled, gated, planned space. The gate is the point at which the funeral procession changes register: from street to enclosure. The atlas draws a schematic plan rather than a survey.

The image that survives when the grave does not. Photographs are the atlas’s main evidence for cemeteries and memorials, and also its main source of error: a photograph documents a moment of maintenance, not a state. The portrait on a headstone is a different object again, and one the atlas has not been able to document.

A painted image of a holy figure or feast, used in worship and in the funeral rite. The Last Judgment icon is the atlas’s central image of the afterlife: a diagram of judgement with inscribed compartments. The Dormition icon supplies the model of the good death. Both are shown as historical objects, not as illustrations of doctrine.

Covered in the house after a death in many recorded accounts. The practice is widely reported; the explanation is not stable, and the atlas marks the chronology of the custom as unknown. It is included in the object index because it is the most frequently cited material sign of the threshold.

The low metal or wooden fence around a plot. A ubiquitous feature of Russian cemeteries in the twentieth century, and almost entirely absent from the sources used here. The atlas notes it as an object that everyone has seen and no one has documented.

A state-built ensemble commemorating collective death. From the late 1950s the Soviet state built large ensembles — Piskaryovskoye, Mamayev Kurgan, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier — that combined architecture, sculpture, landscape and ceremony. They are documents of how the state wanted the dead to be seen.

A continuously burning flame at a memorial. The flame on the Field of Mars in Leningrad was lit in 1957; the flame at Piskaryovskoye was lit from it at the memorial’s opening in 1960. The flame is a technology of memory: it requires maintenance, and its maintenance is the state’s promise.

The bundle of dress for one’s own burial, prepared in life and stored. In many households dress for the dead was prepared during life and stored: linen, a shirt or dress, stockings, sometimes a shroud. It is known by different names in different places. The plate reports the practice as the ethnography describes it, without a count of households.

A ring of flowers or branches, thrown into rivers at Semik or set on roadside signs and graves. At Semik, wreaths and birches were thrown into rivers, and in some readings whether a wreath floated or sank signalled marriage or death (encyclopedia entry, regions named without original records). On roadside memorial signs Matlin counts wreaths among the cemetery-like forms. The atlas notes that the plastic wreath of the modern cemetery is visible everywhere and documented in its sources almost nowhere.

A ritual exit and entrance between this world and the other, in a study of the Eastern Slavs. Lewkijewskaja reads the window as the route by which the souls of the dead, and mythological figures, enter and leave the house, and throwing something out of it as a way of disposing of a dangerous or impure thing. Andryunina reports doors and windows opened at a death in western fringe regions. Only the first author’s abstract was read, and her study generalises across all the Eastern Slavs, so it frames the question and does not describe a village.

A memorial placed where a person died on the road; Matlin counted 299 on three highways. Matlin sorts the signs into two families: one imitates the cemetery with crosses, steles, obelisks, fenced plots and wreaths; the other does not, and uses flowerpots, gazebos, decorated trees and car parts. Placement differs by region. The survey covers three routes in three neighbouring republics, and the lifespan of the temporary items could not be established.
Offering for the domovoy · ugoshchenie domovomu

Food and sweets left for the spirit of the house, and tables not left empty overnight. Ansimova and Golubkova report that food was set out for the domovoy at commemorations of dead parents. Granova’s informants in Severny Kommunar say sweets are left for him and tables are not left empty overnight, and a fixed formula is spoken to take him to a new house. Her study rests on one village and gives the beliefs as much reduced.

A stake reported in borderland records as marking or fixing the grave of a suicide or a sorcerer. Ovseichik reports that the body of a suicide was sometimes marked with an aspen stake, and that radical measures against sorcerers included driving an aspen stake through the body; he cites one modern informant for the latter. The atlas gives these as reports from one borderland. They are not instructions and not a general rule.
Overturned tables and benches · oprokinutye stoly i lavki

Tables and benches turned over before the washing of the body, in an account taken from earlier ethnographers. Rouhier-Willoughby writes that the women who washed the body turned tables and benches over before washing them, so that death would enter the soil; she draws this from earlier ethnographers, so it reaches the atlas at second hand. A hieromonk calls turning over tables and chairs a pagan survival with nothing in common with the Orthodox rite.

A gravestone found serving as a curb or road material, in reports from Moscow. Minkin reports gravestones found used as curbs near the Estrada Theatre on Bersenevskaya Embankment in 2019, known through a municipal deputy’s photographs, with some stones still showing dates of birth and death. Statements that granite from cemeteries was reused for roads in the 1920s and 1930s come from a quoted architect and a state enterprise and are marked unverified; no decision or archive is cited.
Memorial page or account · memorial’naia stranitsa

The online page or account of a dead person, as studied in two abstracts. Linden studies online commemoration by virtual ethnography of three memorial sites and social networking sites, and argues that online tools enable communal remembrance. Sergeeva, Gerlit and Krcmar expect services to host more deceased than living users in the coming decades and heirs to find it hard to identify all accounts. Both are abstract-only readings, and no profile or message of a dead person is reproduced in the atlas.
AI avatar of the dead · ai-avatar

A digital recreation of a dead person’s voice and habits, described by researchers. A university news item reports HSE researchers describing AI avatars of the dead, which can recreate voice and habits and can also produce errors, with a comparison to Frankenstein’s creature. They say such tools can support a sense of connection and can also delay acceptance of loss. The atlas has the news item, not the article, and leaves both effects open.

The border between the living and the dead, maintained by prohibitions rather than by a wall. Used for the set of small adjustments made around a death: the opened window, the covered mirror, the water thrown out, the body carried out. The term is analytical; the sources describe the practices, not the concept.

The part of the person that survives death; described in both theological and folk registers. Orthodox doctrine and folk belief use the same word (dusha) for different constructions: a created immortal substance judged by God, and a breath-like presence that lingers near the body and must be fed and escorted. The atlas keeps the registers apart.

The dead coming back, or being treated as if they might. The returning dead are a way of talking about unfinished obligation. The atlas distinguishes the ethnographic reports (documented) from the category built on them (interpretation).

The washing of the body and the separation of the living from the dead. Washing is both practical and symbolic. The atlas treats it as a technique for handling the dead at arm’s length, and avoids claims about its pre-Christian origin.

The social and emotional work of loss, performed in public or withheld. In the Russian twentieth century mourning was repeatedly reorganised: by the Church, by the Soviet state and by the family. The atlas follows the distinction between public commemoration and private grief.

The scheduled repetition of prayer, food and naming. Remembrance in this atlas is a calendar and a set of objects: days three, nine and forty, the annual commemoration, the meal, the name spoken aloud. It is the most documented form of relation with the dead.

The use of the dead by the living — personal, familial, national. Memory is treated here as a practice with owners and budgets. The state’s memory is built at memorial complexes; the family’s memory at the table and at the grave.

The state of a grave, a cemetery or a name that no one maintains. Abandonment is what memory turns into when nobody tends it. The atlas documents it as a condition of the material record, and marks its own inability to survey it.

The imagined geography of the dead. The atlas distinguishes the doctrinal claim (judgement, resurrection, communion with God) from the iconographic and folk geography (scales, rivers of fire, roads, places of waiting).

What the living owe the dead, and what an unpaid obligation is believed to produce. Used for the reading, offered on plate E and on the table of plate D, that burial, washing, feeding and commemoration are obligations that can be discharged or left unpaid. The term is analytical; plate E marks the "unpaid debt" reading as the atlas’s own interpretation, not a folk category.

The fixed days on which the dead are commemorated, and the ways the church and the village count them differently. Covers the third, ninth and fortieth days, the parental Saturdays, Radonitsa, Semik and the Saturdays before Pokrov and St Demetrius. Plates C and U separate the church rule from local custom; the term only groups them.

A death outside the expected order, and the burial and fear attached to it. Zelenin’s category of the "pledged" dead and the later dispute over it (plates E and T). It is a scholarly construction on real reports, not a taxonomy the sources show villagers sharing.

The afterlife of stone, timber and ground once the dead are no longer tended. Gravestones as curbs and foundations, churches as crematoria, houses left standing. Plates K, W and M record cases; reuse here names a pattern across them, not a single policy.

A being tied to a house and its occupants, whose relation to the dead is disputed. The domovoy of plate S. Whether it is read as an ancestor is a question the sources answer differently; the atlas keeps the limit of that reading visible.

One body, name or place standing in for many that cannot be handled individually. The unknown soldier, the mass grave, the memorial that carries a figure instead of a register (plates I and L). The term names the exchange of information for ritual focus.

Burial and passage below the surface, in caves, cellars, tunnels and flooded ground. Plates R and Q: the Pechory caves, a legend of a tunnel, drowned settlements. Descriptions of what lies below are marked by whether anything was surveyed or only reported.
Vagankovo (plague dead, 1771); the Donskoy crematorium (1927); Novodevichy, the Soviet state necropolis; the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier (1967).
Smolensk cemetery (the 1881 memorial-meal photograph); Piskaryovskoye Memorial Cemetery (1960); the Field of Mars flame (1957).
Kazan cemetery: a roofed grave-cross (golubets) photographed in 2013. Shown with St Petersburg on the map.
Icons of the Last Judgment from the 1540s, recorded as coming from the Nativity monastery; the Dormition icon from the Desyatinny monastery.
The region in which E. V. Barsov recorded the laments published in Prichitaniia Severnogo kraia (1872–1886).
Provenance of the eighteenth-century Last Judgment icon (1770s–1780s) used in plate H.
Mamayev Kurgan, the memorial complex on the site of the Stalingrad fighting.
Nizhne-Gnilovskoye cemetery: a photographed abandoned tomb, released under CC0. Used as the atlas’s single image of abandonment.
A documented commemoration at graves, photographed in 2014. Included as a regional example and explicitly not as evidence for Russian practice.
Two photographed city cemeteries, Zaretskoe (2019) and Besovets (2022).
A photographed bog in Karelia, used on plate O. The marker stands at the district centre, not at the lake.
Sredny Island, Keret Archipelago · Russian Federation
A photographed abandoned cemetery on a White Sea island, used on plate W. The marker is the island’s research station.

A wooden roadside cross photographed at the turn to Reshma, used on plate P. The marker stands at the regional centre; the exact site is not placed here.

An abandoned log house photographed in 2008, used on plate A. The marker stands at the regional centre; the village is not placed here.
An abandoned wooden house by a country road, photographed in 2016, used on plates L and M. The site within the oblast is not stated; the marker stands at the regional centre.
A monastery built over burial caves near the Estonian border; the subject of plate R.
A town at the confluence of the Mologa and the Volga, now under the Rybinsk Reservoir. Coordinates are approximate.
Resettlement from the flood zone, as described in an article on this district. The marker stands at the city.
The day of Semik given to the drowned in Vyatka, in the encyclopedia’s account. The marker stands at the city, and the province was far larger.
Fieldwork on funeral practice in one district, and a Semik custom reported for the province. The marker stands in the district.

Beliefs about the domovoy recorded in one village in June 2019, one village only.
Commemoration days recorded for the Komi-Permyaks, a people who are not Russian. Used on plate U only as a regional comparison. The marker stands at Kudymkar.
One of two regions of fieldwork on the main cemetery commemoration. The marker stands at the regional centre.
The second region of the same fieldwork. The marker stands at the regional centre.
Sections of three federal highways in Chuvashia, Tatarstan and Mordovia, surveyed for roadside memorial signs. The marker is the centre of the three republics, not a route.
One of the three regions of the borderland material on the ‘impure’ dead. Belarusian, so not evidence for Russian practice by itself.
Cemetery demolition as reported in a 2023 interview: dated local decisions of 1920, 1929 and 1930 (the old cemetery became a garden, later a park). Interviewee’s account, no archive cited.
